utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did not receive interpretation, and I am on number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can follow the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I take it there are no problems with the interpretation. No? Are there any problems with the interpretation? I'm not asking you, Mr. Brdjanin. I think I better stop it here because it's getting complicated. Appearances, Ms. Korner. If at any time, Mr. Brdjanin, you can't follow the proceedings in your own language, please draw my attention. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Denise Gustin, case manager, Ann Sutherland, and Joanna Korner. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is John Ackerman. I'm the lead counsel for Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. Also present in this Courtroom are my esteemed colleagues David Cunningham from Houston, Texas, and Aleksandar Vujic from Belgrade, former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to you, too. I understand there's a preliminary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Only one, Your Honour. Your Honour will recall some time ago, I think we were required by Your Honours, or somebody, to supply copies of all the documents referred to by Mr. Brown in his report, but not specifically exhibited, so we've done that. They are on a set of CDs, four in all, which we will hand up. Mr. Ackerman has already got his set. And if somebody can come and collect them. And can I make the whole set attached to the exhibit that was the report, it will be P2416.2. .1 was already the correction that Mr. Brown made, and if anybody wants to use them and give them a separate exhibit number later, that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The sooner we finish this case, the better, Ms. Korner, Mr. Ackerman, because I'm running out of space in my Chamber. I haven't got any more space where I -- to put documents, this case and other cases. It's becoming impossible. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Anything else before we usher the witness in? Yes, usher, you could escort the witness, please. It's a good thing you're using this medium because otherwise it would become even more impossible with the documents that come in in this case, and in other cases. It's...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think the ICTY must have destroyed at least two or three rainforests during the course of its existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only other case in my life when I had this was a big bank fraud case that lasted three months. You know, I had a room full of documents obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Professor Shoup.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that you have a problem with a binder that you should have but you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't. It's not urgent, but I don't know what the procedures are since I'm not supposed to be in contact with the Defence attorney. But I did leave something over there on Monday, and I'm just passing you a note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Hackworth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, John.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm Mr. Hackworth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are Mr. Hackworth? Professor Shoup is informing me that he has left a 61-page binder in your office, and he would like to have it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With Your Honours permission, I would have it delivered to the desk at his hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So good afternoon to you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. We will be proceeding with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your direct. May I just remind you that you're still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Hackworth or Ackerman will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, my, I'm hopeless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will be putting some further questions. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ackerman: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can call me any name you wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We have a ways to go as you know. I need you to have -- I hope you have brought with you the notebook that has the exhibits in it.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. No, I didn't. But... I expect that I have questions that will be asked from the exhibit notebook?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll still get there. It's just going to take us quite a bit longer. I need you to be shown an exhibit, DB195, please. And we don't have them in the courtroom even?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do have. If it helps -- if it assists you in proceeding faster, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really think in terms of getting through this, it's going to be a lot faster if we take like a 15-minute break and let Professor Shoup -- his hotel is just across the street. Let him go over there and get the document and bring it back. I think that will actually save us time in the long run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to use the documents that you indicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are available here, and I can let him have mine. We are share, Judge Janu with me, and Judge Taya, with me, and we can proceed without losing any minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, we can try it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I am familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document you have before you, sir, is DB195. It is a regular combat report, JNA 5th Corps command, 26 March 1992.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only portion of that document that I'm interested in bringing to your attention is on the second page under "state of morale"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will see the language, "All unanimously believe that withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina should not be allowed at any price."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the end of what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I have about that is to you, in terms of your knowledge of what was going on in March in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to you, what significance, if any, does that passage have?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. The date of this document, as I understand it, is March 26th, 1992, prior to the outbreak of the war on April 6th and 7th. This to me is really a cry of pain, in a way, because these are soldiers who have probably been fighting in Croatia up until that time and have now -- they are part of the 5th Krajina Corps, I assume, of the JNA and are now back in Bosnia. Most of these soldiers will have been from Bosnia proper because by this time the JNA has been reorganised in such a fashion that those soldiers who are in Bosnia will be from Bosnia. There are others in the ranks of the JNA at this point, and I think there probably are some Muslims as well. And the question that arises is, are these units going to serve to try to maintain stability and peace in Bosnia, or are they there to actually participate in some kind of a coming conflict, on the one side, that is in this case on the side of the Serbs themselves. I frankly cannot tell you when they say they want to stay in Bosnia whether they're thinking either in the first way or in the second way, and my guess is that they are thinking both ways at the same time. They want peace and stability in Bosnia, as most people did; on the other hand, they are ready to use their weapons as they used them against the Croatians, if necessary, against an enemy of the Serbs. That's as far as I can go with that particular document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would ask Mr. Ackerman and the witness that -- to explain, the witness, when he's speculating, as he clearly is here, in our submission, or when he's actually basing what he has to say on some knowledge that he has, from other documents or other sources. Because at the moment, I would object to this on the grounds it seems to me to be pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Shoup, you've taken the message.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I would say this is not pure speculation. There's a statement here that these people want to remain in Bosnia. Their motives are mixed. That is speculation, but it's not speculation in terms of my knowledge of the region and the people. It's very clear they want to stay there, some of them to defend the Serbs in the case of an upcoming war, probably some who are Muslim to serve as a stabilising force. I don't think this is off the top of my head, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document I want you to look at is Exhibit P80, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to draw your attention to Article 35 of this document.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you know from our earlier conversations that this document is the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina adopted on 16th September 1991. And the one portion I want to bring to your attention is the second paragraph of Article 35 which reads: "Decisions and conclusions of the Assembly shall become binding for the associated municipalities once they have been approved by the assemblies of municipalities." Again, based on your knowledge of the political culture of former Yugoslavia, does that particular portion of this document surprise you in any way?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, and it does not. The political culture in Yugoslavia under Tito and the organisation of State organs under the Titoist regime and in Bosnia placed a great deal of stress on the municipalities, that is, the opstinas, they had a great deal of power. And I think as testimony goes forward, we shall see that in this period of confusion within Bosnia, the municipalities acquired even greater power locally. To the point where it's quite possible here, and I will say that I am speculating for the sake of the Prosecutor, because I don't know -- it's not based upon my knowledge of this particular region --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's, I'm afraid, the point I am making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I object to evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- which is based on speculation. Anyone can speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I accept that. I agree. You don't have to go any further with the objection. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Professor Shoup, please restrict yourself to assessments and conclusions that you can base on evidence and on facts, but not on speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. All right. I will just simply then conclude as far as Article 35 is concerned is that what this seems -- no, what it says really is that decisions of the Autonomous Region of Krajina will have to be approved by the municipalities. This does seem to be, and this is not speculation, very much in accord with the way the political system was structured in a Titoist system.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Professor Shoup, first of all, the place we're going to next is some passages from your book that I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I need the usher's assistance. I have a document I'd like the usher to -- Your Honour, I had several copies of these in my briefcase yesterday which are still in my briefcase from yesterday, which is not here. But I have a copy that I want to give to Ms. Korner because I'm going to refer to this document. But I'm not going to use it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is this the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, don't give it to the witness; give it to Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with regard to your book, I just want to begin that process by referring to a review of your book that I've just handed Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's written by Stjepan G. Mestrovic of Texas A&M University. What he says in part of his review is this: "While Burg and Shoup's exceedingly well documented analysis leaves more questions than answers --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please read more slowly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will. I'm sorry. You've got the only copy that I brought, but I can assure you that it's there somewhere. I'm not making this up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "While Burg and Shoup's exceedingly well documented analysis leaves more questions than answers, if all sides were guilty, if the war was mostly local, and if leaders were not in firm control of chains of command or policy, then the implications of speaking about ideas of ethnic cleansing and genocide in this region seem problematic. The reader walks away from this book feeling that chaos reigned, whereas crimes against humanity seem to require some degree of order and clear intent." Would you say this is a fair analysis of your book?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me start my comments by saying that that book has been introduced as evidence, and so the Court itself will be in a position to judge your question as well as I am from their impressions of the book. I was somewhat amused by this comment when I read it in the review because I had a feeling that Mr. Mestrovic was seeking very clear answers to problems in Bosnia, and especially to know who was the good guy and who was the bad guy. And when he didn't find them, he was rather upset. And I must say that this has often been the reaction that we've had to the book itself. By way of sort of consoling Mr. Mestrovic, I don't think there is anything in this book that suggests that policies of ethnic cleansing, for example, were ones that were devised solely at the local level. We speak of how the Serbs, for instance, carried out ethnic cleansing. We never say this was simply done at a whim. We don't even hint at that. And you will see that as the analysis in the book goes forward, we are identifying the motives of the leaders very precisely, be it Karadzic or be it Izetbegovic. And in effect, in doing so, attributing to them the policies that then transpire. Finally, let me just say briefly that so much of the book is devoted to the interplay between the international community on the one hand and these leaders on the other. And we treat these leaders as though they were, in effect, speaking for their particular parties or their particular points of view. I think in doing that, we probably oversimplify the splits within different parties and within different groups. I will end by just saying that some of the material hat we have access to now, the CIA reports and things like this, show a far greater degree of differences within these groups than Professor Burg and I were aware of at the time we wrote the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just kind of a follow-up question, did you find any difference in the degree of organisation depending upon the level of the structures that you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you could clarify that question, if you could give it -- give me a more precise example of what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you just said that the interplay between the international community and the leaders --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- appeared to be -- I don't think these are exactly your words, but well-organised. I'm wondering if you found that kind of organisation at lower structural levels, at the opstina level, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would hesitate to say we did or we did not. Those of you who know the book now know that for the most part we were not dealing with events at that level. I think that I will just have to pass on that particular question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go then to your book, DB1, at page 17.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at page 17, about two-thirds of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to refer you to the following language: "But it was the breakup of Yugoslavia that opened the door to war by forcing the question of self-determination of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its respective nationalities. Bosnia's violent past did heighten fears and produced the mentalities that collapsed communal solidarity over mutual reconciliation. But if Yugoslavia had survived and the issue of self-determination had not arisen, or if the dissolution of Yugoslavia had been managed by international and domestic actors in a manner that resolved the conflicts between republics and nations peacefully, the ethnic communities of Bosnia would in all likelihood have continued to live in peace."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That -- I'm wondering if you can elaborate a bit on that passage, because it tends to be quite conclusory?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it contains several different points here. One is the fact that Bosnia's violent past, as it we put it here, gave rise to fears that if war came to Yugoslavia, or if the question of Yugoslavia's existence came up, that Bosnia would be prone to civil war. We will probably have occasion in the future to discuss this question of this sort of political and social and cultural nature of Bosnia's past, and I don't want to perhaps dwell on it right now. I should say that that fear, that if Yugoslavia broke up and if there was a violence, that Bosnia would break up was one that was well known. There was a report issued by the Central Intelligence Agency of the United States in 1990 which made it very clear that this would be the fate of Bosnia. In fact, it almost predicted that such a civil war was certain. So that on that front, the fear that something terrible could happen in Bosnia, we all, I think -- all of us who knew Yugoslavia anticipated that such a thing could happen. On the second point that's made here, that if Yugoslavia had survived and the issue of self-determination had not arisen, that the ethnic communities of Bosnia would have in all likelihood lived in peace reflects a point that I make in the report, and perhaps it's not necessary to go into this very deeply, we can come back to it, and that is that the relationships between the ethnic communities in Bosnia depended in a crucial way upon the presence of a Yugoslav state to which both the Muslims and the Serbs of Bosnia felt loyalties. I think this is an easy concept to understand, and we don't have to really go back over that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Professor.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We both have to remember to go a great deal slower --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- because --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm deliberate, but not slow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- they are trying to keep up with you --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Fine, okay. Now, the final point here, I think, and then I will be open to more questions is simply that -- and I think it's a terribly important one at the end of the paragraph, we note that the nationalist leaders faced few obstacles to their efforts to play upon fear, to mobilise ethnic solidarity, and thereby to orchestrate the dissent into violence that produced catastrophe for their peoples. Why was it that they didn't face the opposition that one might anticipate? I think this will come up in the questioning, but I would want to say simply this much, and that is that the demise of Yugoslavia was a tragic situation for the Bosnians. It left them with choices that they did not want to make, especially the choice of independence or not. Because faced with that choice, all types of problems then arose, including the national question about which we'll speak, and the nationalist leaders were then perfectly poised to take advantage of that situation. I think that's maybe as far as I'll go for the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, that leads very naturally to my next question, which you'll find raised by a passage on page 5 in the book in the introduction, which you called the second major contest unleashed in Bosnia by the disintegration of Yugoslavia was over the national question. This term is commonly used throughout Eastern Europe, applied to all aspects of interethnic relations, but its most important element concerning defining the right claim, titular or state constituting status usually reserved for the majority ethnic group and defining the rights that accrues to others, minority ethnic groups." You talk there about the national question, and I think again that's a matter that can use a little bit of elaboration.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Using the term national question in the context of the disputes in Yugoslavia is very intentional and very important. When we talk about the national question usually as political scientists, we mean the relationship between the nation and the state and the constitutional issues that arise in this connection. As we mention here, the question of which ethnic community or which nation is the titular nationality, that is the one after which the state may be named and therefore enjoys certain privileges. The question of the rights of minorities, the question of who has the right to, for example, secede from the country. Now, that we would distinguish from the notion of an ethnic dynamic, rivalries between ethnic groups, let's say, in a village or ethnic communities or communal riots. These all are ethnic relationships. And I will also make a distinction in the course of my discussion, I think, between ethnic rivalries and a lesser distinction, that is, between cultural differences such as existed among the peoples of Bosnia. Now, the point that I would like to make, it's my own personal observation, but I think it will be borne out here in the course of our testimony, is this: That the national question, the question of whether a particular ethnic community had the right to enjoy independence, for example, or to claim the right to be the titular nationality was the driving force behind the disintegration of Yugoslavia, and actually although ethnic rivalries were a great problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the national question was also the driving force behind the dissolution of Bosnia itself. That is, the disputes within Bosnia in this particular case of whether there should be a Bosnian state or there should not, whether the Serbs should have the right to secede -- with the Croatians and so forth. And I'll close on this note: It's important to understand that in Tito's Yugoslavia and in Tito's Bosnia, relations among the ethnic communities were not ones of bitter enmity. There were memories of past -- violent clashes during World War II, and we'll talk about that. But what introduced the question of ethnic rivalries and uncertainties was the national question, that is, the secession of Slovenia, the secession of Croatia, and then what followed, the question of should there be a Bosnia or should there not? Therefore, I think the national question as I have just tried to explain what I conceive of it as is to be paramount and central to the whole discussion here about the dissolution of Yugoslavia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to follow up on something you just said. You said the question of should there be a Bosnia or should there not.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that ever an actual question and was that ever a matter of debate, as to whether or not there should be a Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, of course it was a matter of debate. In a sense it always has been, simply because Serb and Croat nationalists from the turn of the 19th century onward always felt that Bosnia, in fact, was either Croatian or Serbian. During World War II, as you know, the Croatian Ustasha fascist government annexed all of Bosnia because they felt it was part of Croatia. And similarly now, the question of whether there should be a Bosnia after Yugoslavia was dissolved was certainly not one that one could just assume as settled. Obviously the Serbs in Bosnia had a different concept; that is, that they had the right to secede. They weren't concerned about what was left, but they certainly felt they didn't belong in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any meetings or discussions or anything of that nature that could have led to the disappearance of Bosnia? I mean, did people sit and talk about that? I mean, people in leadership positions.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that in this -- in -- except to say that the issue for the Serbs and for the -- for one group of the Croatians, of course, was secession from Bosnia. If the Bosnian Muslims chose to still call what was left Bosnia, you know, there was no objection to that. I'm not quite sure that anyone was trying to claim at any point that Bosnia had disappeared. By way of contrast, with Yugoslavia where the Badinter commission said you know that Yugoslavia is in a state of dissolution, although Bosnia had effect ceased to exist by 1991, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back now to Chapter 2 where we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean to say when you say: "Bosnia had in effect ceased to exist by 1991, I would suggest"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me make the point as concisely as I can because I think we'll come back to it. From 1989, as far as I can judge, onward, there was an increasing mobilisation of each of the ethnic communities behind their own leaders, and in certain parts of Bosnia by 1990, the writ of the government didn't run. For example, in the Western Herzegovina, which in effect had set up its own little mini state. Then, after the elections in Bosnia in December of 1990, and now we're back -- we're in January of 1991 roughly. There was a competition between the various ethnic parties within a state itself, that is, the government of Bosnia in Sarajevo, and at the local level. The consequence of that was almost a paralysis of Bosnia. Now, this is an event that has not been, I think, adequately examined or researched, and so I'm not going to tell you that it was true in every case and in every place in Bosnia. I have quoted in my report some observations about how Bosnia in effect had become paralysed by this time because of the ethnic clashes within it. If you interpreted my remarks to mean that legally Bosnia had ceased to exist, no, I didn't mean that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But functionally.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Functionally it had ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Chapter 2, page 16, you begin the chapter basically with this statement: "For most of its history." And I'm not asking for a long answer here

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "For most of its history Bosnian society had been deeply segmented with Muslims, Serbs, and Croats organised into distinct communities." I do want you to talk about that briefly.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Let me answer that question in two ways. By the end of the communist era, roughly 45 years of rule under the communists, many of the distinctions which had been part of the life of Bosnia prior to that time had been leveled between classes and groups. And so one could say that some changes, really very fundamental changes, had taken place in Bosnia. Nevertheless, the residue of those earlier social relationships, cultural, economic, political, which divided the ethnic communities from earlier eras still lingered on in part. Bosnia was, however, segmented in another fashion under the Titoist regime. And I want to make this point because it will come up, I think, in the course of our discussion. It was segmented because it was only a partially developed republic. The differences between the urban and rural areas in Bosnia in the 1990s were extreme. It's really remarkable, for example. Bosnia was segmented by different regions with different traditions, and I make a point of that in the report. Furthermore, you would find that, let's say in perhaps not so much in Bosnia but in neighbouring Croatia, but this is a phenomena I think the Court should consider, the effects of World War II led to different waves of settlers in, let's say, a village where the Germans had left. And there was a term for these new settlers who came. They were quite different from the old settlers. Now, this is a segmentation of a new kind, of course. But the reaction when the crisis came in 1991 and 1992 was far different between the old settlers and the new settlers to the crisis and to the war. So it was the new settlers who had come from Bosnia and Croatia who were the spearhead of the war itself. I've talked longer than you wanted me to, but I do feel that it's important to note that there's a sort of new kind of set of differences that are at work here before the war breaks out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was just sitting here feeling very glad that I had asked for a short answer.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the long answer might be like. All right. I'll be more to the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we do have a time within which we probably need to finish.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's try to -- if I want you to elaborate on an answer, I'll tell you. But let's try to keep the answers a little bit shorter if we can.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the next page, right before the quote we started with --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you tell me the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 17. Right before the quote we started this discussion with, you say this: "The violent history of Bosnia must be taken into account if one is to understand the war and the course it took." Now just very briefly, why? Why do you have that --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, I will be brief. This has been an object of discussion -- a problem that people have discussed. Noel Malcom and others have said, no, it wasn't violent. But first of all, we have to consider the impact of World War II. It has an immense impact on people because of the massacres that took place at that time, even genocide. Most of the people here in the Court know that and I don't have to go into that any further. Secondly, I do think when you talk about the violent history of Bosnia that you should take into account that it was an area under the Ottoman Empire and under the Austrians where the military frontier separated -- or at least under the Ottoman Empire separated the Austrian Empire from the Turks, and this is an area where people lived with the gun, as you know, and this was not just something that one imagined. In this connection, then I'll stop after this, in my report on page 44, 45, I think, there is an account, a brief account, of a feud that took place in Medjugorje, and I think you probably know what I mean. It's an account that was done by a Dutch anthropologist. The viciousness of that feud is absolutely startling, and this was between two Croatian families. It was not ethnic. Not only were they trying to get even with each other, they were hanging each other by their necks, they were slashing each other's throats and so forth. So one can see that there is a cruelty in this rural region of the -- at least in Western Herzegovina. Now, I'll almost stop and say one thing. I do think you just have to be careful not to use this as an explanation for everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. One of the perhaps dilemmas, let me preface the question by asking you this: We've all heard of I think almost at sufficient length, if not at sufficient length about what happened in Bosnia and in the Bosanska Krajina area during World War II. What was the situation between the ethnic groups living in that area in Bosnia, let's say, by 1953? Eight years after World War II.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in that area in 1953, so I have been in Bosnia a few years later, of course, so I can talk -- if we can talk more generally about it. I don't want to pretend that I was in Banja Luka at that particular time. But --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put the question --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can put the question a little differently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little bit differently. Was there anything about the way the Tito regime was structured that affected the relationships between the ethnic groups following World War II?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely. I was in Yugoslavia and briefly in Bosnia in 1952 and 1953 as a student. And this was a time when Yugoslavia's prestige was at an all-time high. Tito was worshipped by all of the Yugoslavs. And the ideology of the regime was overwhelming. People believed that Yugoslavia was representative of the future of socialism, they believed in brotherhood and unity, at least in their everyday life. This was a time when international student groups were always coming to build highways and this kind of a thing in Yugoslavia. There was a great optimism in the country. And I think there was a feeling that those nationalist rivalries had been defeated, at least for the moment. That doesn't mean that people themselves had changed fundamentally underneath. That was the other thing you could observe, as I observed myself. They were fundamentally still Serbs, Croats, Muslims, whatever. There was this deep ethnic identity that they still retained. But the republic rivalries had not yet begun. If you choose 1953, this was a very optimistic time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to all the people who basically led the violence in World War II, the extreme nationalists. Were they still there in 1953?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. And I as a student met them. Chetniks who would come up to and me and want to talk to me about what they had done during World War II. They were there. However, I must say that the leaders themselves were not there. They had been arrested, they had been executed. But you could meet on the streets very easily, and I did very often, you know, persons either in Croatia who had been very violently nationalist or in Serbia. It gave you a rather spooky feeling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But overlying all of it, there seems to have been a peace that differs from what we see today in Bosnia. Do you agree with --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely. Oh, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we are nine years after the war now. Why is it different now than it was in, like, 1953, eight years after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Let me simplify the answer to two points. First of all, I go back to the point I made earlier. The Bosnians were satisfied with their place within Yugoslavia. First of all, they had -- and this was for the Muslims important, a republic of their own. But more importantly, all the Slav Muslims that were within Yugoslavia and so were all of the Serbs. They were comfortable with the constitutional arrangements of that time, and they all genuinely idolised Tito. So this was extremely, extremely important, you see. The other point was that they felt secure. This was a very tough, harsh regime. In Serbo-Croatian you say "cvrsta ruka". You mean firm hand. And that feeling of security was something that was important above all, even in a small village in Krajina or anywhere else, people felt secure. And that you could testify to by going back there yourself and seeing it. And this was -- these are the two things that are lacking now, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Chamber has heard from a number of people from Bosnia that with regard to the places they come here from, the villages they were living in at the time, that everyone was getting along well between the ethnic groups, that relations were good, that in many cases there were mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That people were attending each other's ethnic celebrations.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that the relationships were good between the people. And the question that sort of cries out, I think, from that is how could things have deteriorated so rapidly when the war broke out in 1991?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. First of all, I think it helps to realise that things were not perfect in Tito's Yugoslavia, that rivalries were developing between the republics over economic investments and things of this nature. For example, up until the mid-1960s, Kosovo was actually a police state under Serb control. If anyone had gone down to Kosovo and gotten an authentic reply from an Albanian, they would have told you that they were living under a police state at this time. Splits and fissures within the Yugoslav system were developing already. I noticed that when I was there in the 1950s and 1960s. The point was that this did not at the time affect the daily lives of people, going about their own affairs. And as long as they felt secure and as long as there was a one-party system which would disperse jobs and investments according to some kind of a key along ethnic proportional lines, people in their daily lives, you see, were not perhaps so aware or didn't care really what was going on among the leaderships and so on. This was true all the way up until the outbreak of the war in 1990 and 1991. That's why it took people so much by surprise. Many people just were not keyed in to what was really going on among the leaderships themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go to page 40 of your book, there are a couple of passages that speak to the subject we have been talking about here for the last few minutes. In the first full paragraph after the first sentence: "The ability of the communists to transform Bosnia-Herzegovina into a model of multiethnic, multicultural coexistence after the war was more surprising. The reasons must be sought, above all, in the authoritarian nature of the communist regime which exercised absolute control over the ethnic communities in Bosnia." Then if we skip down a ways: "The remarkable success of the communists in consolidating power in Bosnia must therefore be attributed both to their draconian methods in eliminating the nationalists after the war and the compatibility of their political message with the underlying pro Yugoslav orientation of significant segments of the Bosnian population." Just briefly comment on those passages.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be brief because I think this is precisely the point that I have been trying to make up until now. These were the twin pillars of stability within Bosnia. On the one hand, a regime that was repressive but assured people that they were safe. And the other was the constitutional arrangements which suited the Bosnians perfectly, that is, a Yugoslavia overseeing Bosnia and responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had asked you a bit earlier because I'm still baffled by the difference between 1953 and 1994. If you look at the next page, page 42, the beginning of the last paragraph on that page: "Public manifestations of national intolerance were ruthlessly suppressed by the communist regime." Where that was the case after World War II, it's not the case today, is it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we come back once again to the feeling of deep insecurity that people felt as the war broke out in Bosnia and of course which has now become something different. With ethnic cleansing now, these regions in Bosnia are homogeneous. They don't feel insecurity within their own enclave or entity, but they do feel insecurity as far as the future of their own enclave or entity is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That leads, then, to the next question I want you to talk about. We have been speaking about a certain rigidity that existed during the communist era. All of a sudden, Yugoslavia comes out of that rigidity and holds multiparty elections. What effect did that prior rigid system have on the efforts that then had to be made to try to share power between these what became ethnically based parties?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're referring to Bosnia, not Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is important. Bosnia was -- had a reputation during the Titoist period of being the most doctrinaire and rigid republic within Yugoslavia. They did not allow any kind of a dissident movement such as in Croatia -- not in Croatia so much, but in Slovenia or even in Belgrade where intellectuals were quite independent by the 1980s. The consequence of that was that political differences were pretty much kept out of the public eye. Infighting did occur within the communist party of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the late 1980s, and it had a very destructive effect on the party, but it was not something that translated itself into a dynamism of change and reform. Perhaps the more important point is that there was never a dissident movement in Bosnia which could have reached over the ethnic barriers, you know, in an effort to establish more freedom or respect for human rights and so on. If there had been such a movement, such as in Slovenia, for example, perhaps when the elections came you would have seen a more powerful reform party which included all of the three ethnic communities as gaining support -- at least in the urban areas of Bosnia. Finally, just a simple point on that, is because of that rigidity within the Bosnian regime, they simply were not ready when it came after the elections to learn the art of how to accommodate one another. It was a winner take all kind of situation, really. They had never learned any other way of doing things in politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as we get into the Netherlands institute materials, I think we'll see some examples of that. At the time that the League of Communists was basically coming apart, and it looked like there were going to be the development of a multiple multiparty system, was there any concern regarding the danger of ethnically based parties being established?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia? Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course there was. And the first reaction of the League of Communists of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to try to hold snap elections before such parties might form, and then to pass an electoral law which banned national parties from participating in the elections. Both of these efforts failed. We perhaps don't have to go into detail as to why that happened right now. And again, just simply to observe very broadly, I think there was a real dread, a real terrible fear among these --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. There was a real fear of what would happen, you know, if all of a sudden elections were simply dominated by national groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I did raise this yesterday but all of this has been dealt with and effectively Professor Shoup is saying more or less the same thing in Dr. Donia's report, in his evidence. If you look at page 26 of Dr. Donia's report, it's all there, slightly less -- more summary form. But is there really a necessity for us to go through this all over again? To Your Honours -- really the question is, do Your Honours feel you're being assisted by listening to this again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I better not say too much, to be frank, because there were moments, especially yesterday when I was doubting whether we were dealing with the Brdjanin case or some other case. So I'm being very patient because that's in my style, not to disrupt much at this stage. But we could restrict the questions and the answers to what is pertinent to this case, I think we will move ahead quick and in a more pragmatic manner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I leave it in the hands of Mr. Ackerman. I think he knows exactly pretty well what I mean. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go now to page 63 of your book.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we're now in Chapter 3, which is entitled "The Descent into War." There are a couple of -- there are about three things there that I want to refer to and have you talk a little bit about. You say that -- and I'm right at the bottom of page 63, the last few lines.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The government in Sarajevo became to be largely under SDA control. Since Bosnia-Herzegovina was a highly centralised state, the danger was real that SDA and the Muslim ethnic community would effectively shut out the other ethnic communities from power, at least at the level of the central government." Now, how is it that the SDA, that the government in Sarajevo was able to be controlled, as you say, at this stage by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I think maybe this oversimplifies the situation. I'll be brief again. But this is the period between the elections of December 1990 and April 4th of 1992 when Izetbegovic, in effect, declares mobilisation and the Serbs leave Sarajevo. After April 4th of 1992, there's no question about who is in charge. What I'm saying here is that the traditions in Bosnia were such that centralised government called the tune. And the Serbs had every reason to think that -- that the Bosnian government would fall under Muslim control. Let me just give you an example of what you mean, and I'll be brief about it. First, all of the opstinas of Sarajevo had a majority of Muslims, except one, Pale. And so the -- as the struggle for power at the municipal level went forward, of course the Muslims gained control of these different opstinas. But secondly, and more important, if you look at the record in the spring of 1992 before April 4th, you see that Izetbegovic as president is acting in effect for the government of Bosnia. He's making decisions. And this -- although there's a collective presidency of seven people, the others really are shut out completely. And in dealing with the international community and in other respects, dealing with the JNA, the army and so forth, it is Izetbegovic who is speaking for the government of Bosnia. But just briefly, the other point is the fear that the Serbs had, that centralised government is -- traditionally a centralised government would ultimately just leave them out in the cold.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very next passage, then, speaks about what was going on at the same time outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that: "The Serb SDS consolidated its power where the Serbs were a majority. On the eve of the war in spring of 1992, there were reports that the SDS had purged local governments in Serb-majority areas and was insisting that the tangible assets of the community be divided among the ethnic communities."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak about the assets of a community being divided, what kind of assets are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, again, I'm not -- I wasn't watching all of this happen in person. But you could by reading the newspapers at the time get some idea of what was going on. First of all, one of the favorite targets would be the local gas stations, you know, things that had some kind of a municipal -- were dependent upon the municipality and were there for easy things to divide among the various people, various kiosks, or even things as simple as that. But more importantly, I think, was the fact that the entire socialist sector that fell under the control of the municipality, a factory, maybe, maybe a very important factory, was either under the control of the local government or was slated for eventual privatisation. And everyone knew that the party that could control the local government could then control who was going to end up with that particular enterprise or whatever it might be at any given point. And finally, you have such things as the local newspapers, the local -- if there was a TV station, these as well were all up for grabs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, putting it in classic terms, there were a lot of spoils to go to the victors?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. And I haven't even mentioned the posts within the municipal government itself, which were always a bone of contention, how many -- how many -- which party would get to monopolise those jobs. This was a very, very tense, difficult kind of confrontation that went on between the ethnic communities within a given municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next sentence I think you try to give an example of this process: "In Gorazde, the Muslim SDA began a process of weeding out Serbs from responsible positions. According to Serb accounts, the Muslim mayor of Gorazde set to work polarising relations between the ethnic communities. His efforts were opposed by an ethnically mixed committee of intellectuals who tried to contain ethnic tensions in the town. Nonetheless, by the third week of March, Gorazde was a divided city crisscrossed by barricades."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That account was based upon what we knew when we wrote --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please make pauses between question and answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That passage that you read was written back in 1988 [sic], 1999, Professor Burg and I had access to certain documents. We indicate where we got our information. And I would simply say that that has been confirmed, our view of this situation, by a much more detailed analysis of the situation in Srebrenica and Gorazde by Professor Duijzings' contribution to the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation study. The two accounts parallel each other. So I think that that description is quite accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I want to go now to your report, Professor. Talk about it for a while.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think as we begin to talk about your report, I think it might be helpful for you to tell the Trial Chamber how you approached the task of preparing your report in this case.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the Court has seen, this material in the report is drawn first and foremost from the book, highlighting and condensing points the made there about the history of Bosnia. The second thing that I attempted to do was to introduce materials from newly published sources, which are very important for the Bosnian conflict. And those are basically three, the most important of which is the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation study which, of course, an immense study and it's only available in English in an electronic fashion. So I had to take things selectively from that which I thought might be most interesting to the Court. The second new source of great importance is the two-volume study by the CIA called "Balkan Battlegrounds", and the third is a book by Gow on Serbian policy towards Bosnia which I wasn't able to use very much; it simply didn't work out as well as I had thought. The second -- the next thing that I wanted to do was to raise certain issues that I knew were contentious or should be discussed by the Court, and that's why I have done this, discussing such things as the responsibility for ethnic cleansing and the nature of the war, nature of ancient hatreds, drawing on some of the sociological and anthropological literature. And especially I would focus, I would say, on the question of the victimisation strategies which I don't think has ever been discussed before in a scholarly fashion and simply introduced the subject itself, If you looked at the report, you will know what I am referring to. I do want to just say one more point, make one more point about the report, and that is that there is a problem in the scholarly world, first of all, that if we become too interested in presenting every side of the case, that somehow we are getting to the point where we are not blaming anybody for anything. And I just want to make clear absolutely hat this was not my intention certainly, and if we are going to deal with ethnic conflicts where there is usually a problem of exceeding or breaking norms of international behaviour on both sides, we just have to get used to this fact that we can't identify one side as the good side and one as the bad side. And finally, just one point in the report, I suggest that we all really have to become comfortable with the Balkans. We can't pretend that the Balkans are not the Balkans. I say that because I think there is a tendency in the scholarly world, and I even see it in the Dutch report to pretend that this -- what was happening in this region is somehow, well, it happens everywhere; no, we all are prone to violence and so on. And I just think the Balkans has a unique history, we have to understand it, and we have to come to terms with it, without in any way relaxing our standards and criteria of what would be considered to be acceptable behaviour in any conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go, then, to page 3 of your report. The top of the page. You say: "The place to begin is with Yugoslavia. The country was, despite its initial successful in uniting the south Slavs, beset by a number of contradictions. The first was the inherently unstable and perhaps contradictory nature of the contract, if we may call it that, among the peoples who were linked in a common state. The second, the authoritarian means which were employed to paper over these ambiguities both before and after World War II, and the third, failure to create a common state ideology for the south Slav peoples comprising Yugoslavia." Now, we've talked already today about the first two of those to some extent, I think. But the third of those we've not, and there are contradictions here, and I will invite you to comment on those, but not at great length, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the third, you mean the failure to establish a Yugoslav ideology?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I will be brief. Professor Donia -- I'm a political scientist. Professor Donia is a historian. He has probably spoken to these matters. There was at the turn of the century a genuine and authentic pro-Yugoslav sentiment in the south Slav lands. And that contributed to the creation of the Yugoslav State. If you read Rebecca West's book, "Black Lamb and Grey Falcon" you will meet some individuals in that book who genuinely believed in Yugoslavia as such. Then in 1929 when the dictatorship was established by King Aleksandar, you also see, although with a Serb angle if we can put it this way, an effort to try to preserve Yugoslavia as a state, as a notion which had substance beyond and above the national feelings of each of the major nationalities. I would not like to go further except to say that that effort was, again, made by the communists after World War II. It failed in the 1960s. My first book on communism and the national question talks about that failure. And with your permission, I would just like to read what I think is a very poignant remark by Tito. This is in the 1960s about the fact that people don't feel like themselves as Yugoslavs. But with your permission. Here, he is. This is in 1963 after his efforts to try to make people think like Yugoslavs failed. And he says to his fellow party members, he says: "There are even people who don't dare call themselves Yugoslavs," he says. And then he goes on: "I have received these days quite a few letters just in connection with this question of nationality, and mostly from children. Children understand what I am talking about. One little girl from Macedonia, student in the fourth or fifth grade whose father is a Slovenian and mother is a Macedonia has written me, saying she is happy she can now be called a Yugoslav. Look, comrades, a little girl. She wrote it in her own hand. That shows you better than anything how absurd it is to force someone to belong to a nationality, Serb, Croat, or Slovene." And of course he is pleading in vain for people to begin to think like Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go now to page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go now to page 5 of your report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it might be helpful to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what we're doing

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It might be more helpful to the people in the booth if after I ask you a question, you just wait a few seconds before you start answering it. And then maybe pause at the end of each sentence.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're speaking of -- on page 5 of -- you refer to nuances that you've spoken about in the previous sentence. These nuances set the stage for a dysfunctional relationship between Serbs and Croats in Bosnia on the one hand and their respective parent countries bordering on Bosnia, Serbia, and Croatia on the other. "Serbs and Croats in Bosnia were prone to look to Belgrade and Zagreb respectively for leadership, and to favour secession from Bosnia in times of crisis." Of the three peoples there in Bosnia, Serbs and Croats and Muslims, I think what you're saying is the Serbs could look to Serbia in a time of crisis; the Croats could look to Croatia in a time of crisis, but where were the Muslims to look?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I'll pause for a moment. Yes, that's correct. I also want to make a different point, which is very central to the war in Bosnia. And that is that the relationship between the capital, let's say Belgrade and the Serbs in Bosnia is always tense, and it is tense because Milosevic, for example, has an overriding priority which is to pursue his own interests, which relate to Serbia itself. And over and over again, he has to remind these people, the Serbs in Croatia or Bosnia, that the interests of Belgrade and the interests of Serbia come first. Now, I'll just give you one previous but very poignant example and not go further for the moment: In Croatia, an agreement was reached that the United Nations forces, UNPROFOR, would come to occupy those Serbian minority areas, as we all know. The Serbian leadership, and you have someone here who is testifying now, Babic, against this was aghast at this particular moment. And Milosevic wrote him and said, "You have got to understand, Milan," he said, "The interests of the matsa [phoen]," that is Serbia itself, "come first." And this is what governs all of his actions throughout the entire war. He is ready to dispose of these people in Croatia if they don't serve his interests. It comes down to that in Bosnia as well at the end of the war. And this is the tension that I think is very important to understanding the way the war goes in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the questions that has been contended here in this Tribunal since its beginning was the question of whether or not an effort was being made to create what is referred to as a Greater Serbia. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, of course. I think first there is some -- there is a need to be cautious about the use of that term. The Serb intellectuals associated with the memorandum of the Serbian Academy, for example, on -- where everyone sort of goes to start explaining about the notion of a Greater Serbia, never themselves laid out a plan for a Greater Serbia, and more importantly still, were quite ready to accept the notion of a federation within which the Serbs would be a member. As a way of making sure that all Serbs remained in one state; in other words, they were not wedded to the notion of a Greater Serbia territorially. Their goal was something else. It was to make sure that all Serbs would be in one state. So the more radical position was, and I consider that to be the position of espousing a Greater Serbia, was the idea of territorial aggrandizement for Serbia pure and simple, and the extreme right under Seselj and others proposed such projects for the expansion of Serbian territory all the way up to Zagreb and things of this nature. There's a very great difference between these two positions. Secondly, and then I will bring this to a close, those Serbs in, for example, in Bosnia or in Croatia who desperately wanted to join Serbia, they were not opposed to the notion of a Greater Serbia; they were -- in their way extremely wedded to the notion of a national state with all of its symbols and things like this. But their primary concern was to become part of Serbia, not to create a Greater Serbia. Let me just briefly comment on this. Those persons, for example, the Bosnian Serbs in the area you're interested in, in the Krajina, were not particularly eager or concerned about the fate of Kosovo, as you might expect, if they were wedded completely to the notion of a Greater Serbia, and vice versa. They were, of course, extreme in their nationalism, but they were not really, I would say, die-hard proponents of the notion of a Greater Serbia. Milosevic himself distinguished himself from those who espoused a Greater Serbia at various stages of his career and during the war in Bosnia. I won't go into that in great detail now. I've talked enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This might be an appropriate time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you, Professor Shoup. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, we have to be kind to the translators.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we also need to move along a little more quickly or we'll never finish.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to refer, I'm still in your report, I'm on page 5. I'm about two-thirds of the way down. You've written this sentence: "If the breakup of Yugoslavia was attended by violence, then the outbreak of a civil war in Bosnia was virtually unavoidable.". Why do you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I sometimes feel that people who viewed the war in Bosnia were very detached and unrealistic about what they saw. If the rest of Yugoslavia had become violent, let's say, in this case, the war between Serbia and Croatia, if there was a euphoristic nationalism spreading through Yugoslavia, which was the case in the late 1980s, in Slovenia, in Croatia, and of course in Serbia, then it is absolutely impossible to think that this would not spread to Bosnia. This is as simply as I can put it. Now, there are other factors involved. For example, and I'll be quick, when the war broke out between Serbia and Croatia, paramilitaries were attracted to the area. When the United Nations then came in as a peacekeeping force, those paramilitaries and others had no place to go and went to Bosnia. They were a disruptive force. They were looking for a new war. All of that might have been avoided if there had been a peaceful resolution of the conflict between Serbia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 6, you talk about -- I think where you are in that second paragraph on page 6 is,"as war the breaking out", we're in maybe April of 1992. You have this to say -- and we had talked earlier about everyone was getting along extremely well in former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia, and then all of a sudden everything came apart. You wrote this: "While the Bosnian Muslims called for tolerance, they also labelled Serbs on the opposite side of the barricades as Chetniks. Serbs were easily convinced that Muslims were infiltrated by Mujahedin and were bent on creating a Muslim state. The Croats of Western Herzegovina were tagged as Ustasha. These perceptions, it should be added, were not simply manufactured by the nationalist leaderships, although propaganda was rife on all sides, but had a deep resonance thanks to Bosnia's past among the Bosnian people at large." Now, are you saying there that some of this kind of rhetoric that developed and the behaviour that followed it was almost indigenous? It didn't take much to bring it to the surface? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not take much to bring it to the surface if you realise that in intimate conversations among Serbs, among Croats, the notion that the Ustasha were still out there someplace or that they had done these things to Serbs during the war and down the line, the same kinds of references were still very much alive. In daily life, under Tito, it didn't matter. But when Titoism collapsed, what communism collapsed, I guess I would put it this way: The past captured the present. Now you had to think in those terms, and these were terms that you had actually used, discussed, talked about in the intimacy of your kitchen as I've heard these conversations over and over again, even in times of peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had talked about the formation of the ethnic-based parties, the SDA, the SDS, the HDZ. Of course, there were -- political campaigns went on, leading up to the elections. On page 14 of your report, you describe -- and you're quoting from the Netherlands Institute materials at this point, but you describe a rally that was held on the 10th of September 1990 in Velika, Kladusa, and it's described by the Netherlands report in the following language: "On 10 September 1990, the largest SDA rally in the election campaign in Velika Kladusa pushed Zulfikarpasic over the edge." Now let me pause. We heard a little bit about him in the tape yesterday. Tell the Chamber who was Zulfikarpasic and what role did he play as these things developed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zulfikarpasic was a wealthy businessman, a Bosnian Muslim who lived in Zurich who had witnessed atrocities committed in World War II when he was a young man. He came back to Bosnia to try to be to a moderating influence. He joined the SDA party, that is, the Muslim party, then left that party because he found it too extreme. What I did not know until I read this account of the Velika Kladusa rally was that this particular moment played a role in Zulfikarpasic decision. He felt that the SDA was too extreme. And then went forward to try to form a more moderate Muslim party which participated in the elections but didn't get the vote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would have been the MBO?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: MBO, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continuing, then. On what Duijzings says here: "In the presence of at least 200.000 people, the party made it clear that the Muslims were not prepared to live in a rump Yugoslavia, and that if needs be, they would take up arms to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were hundreds of green flags, people in Arabic dress and portraits of Saddam Hussein, people were chanting long live Saddam Hussein, and we're going to kill Vuk," and it in brackets it says Draskovic. Who was Vuk Draskovic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vuk Draskovic was a political leader in Serbia, also a novelist, and he had written novels about World War II, Muslims versus Serbs. So these people are reacting to what they consider him to be a nationalist, a Serb nationalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continuing: "After this, Zulfikarpasic no longer trusted Izetbegovic. And on 18 September, along with a few allies, just about a week later in other words, he and Muhamed Filipovic left the SDA." Now, the Muhamed Filipovic that is mentioned here, the Trial Chamber is familiar with two Muhamed Filipovics. There's one who was from Kljuc, and there's one who was a professor in Sarajevo. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the professor from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This rally with 200.000 people there that this passage describes, would this have happened in a vacuum so that no one outside Velika Kladusa would have known about this?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I wasn't present in Yugoslavia at that particular moment, but I can tell you this would have been -- the news of this would have spread far and wide. It would have had a -- confirmed the views of suspicious Serbs that they and the Muslims were going on divergent paths.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The quote says this rally caused Zulfikarpasic to no longer trust Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what it was that Izetbegovic did, if anything, at that rally that would have caused Zulfikarpasic not to trust him any longer?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I don't think -- I'll be quiet, I'll be just slower. Yes, I do. I don't think in the quote in the report, but if you continue to read Professor Duijzings' account, you will see that Zulfikarpasic says, "We will fight for a Bosnia in which Muslims --" I won't give you the exact phrase; I don't have it in front of me, perhaps you do. But we will fight to -- if we have to, we will fight to make sure that Bosnia is an independent state. And I forget what he says about the Muslim role. But I think this belligerent tone was for Zulfikarpasic a sign that Izetbegovic, posing as a moderate, in fact was ready to go to the extreme extent necessary in this case to achieve his goals. I'm sorry, I can't give you the exact quote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm going to back up a second to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I'm going to back up just a second to -- I think it's page 17 of your report. There was a provision in the 1974 constitution for the creation, I think, according to what you've written here, for a council of national equality. Actually, it was an amendment well after 1974. But it was an amendment to create a -- this national equality council. Do you have any idea why that council of national equality never got off the ground, why it was never actually formed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That body was provided for in an amendment to the constitution that was adopted in 1990. It should have been put into effect even before the elections of late 1990. I have asked my scholar colleagues in Sarajevo to provide me with more information about this constitutional issue unsuccessfully so far. In brief, I can't give you a real answer. My suspicion is that neither the Serbs, nor the Muslim parties were really interested in forming this body and engaging in what would have been a consociational accommodational dialogue to save Bosnia. And let me make one point. What they were doing was dividing the assets of Bosnia between them. That was what they liked to do.
