They were not interested in sitting down and making constitutional arrangements that would make Bosnia function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we can avoid the point that I am objecting to by saying "my suspicion is" rather than "my speculation is."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner, you are perfectly right. What puzzles me, Professor Shoup, is something, just having followed what you just stated, at the same time reading through your report, also your book, and Professor Donia's report, and of course my own personal knowledge of the events, how do you reconcile this with the Serbs then and the Croats trying to partition Bosnia which would have suited both the Serbs and the Croats, but certainly not the Muslims with whom you're saying that the Serbs were very much interested in splitting, sharing, grabbing the assets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You will have noticed that in our book that there was a moment after the elections when the three nationalist parties were getting along very well with one another. The immediate reason for that was that they were all anti-communists, and so they were enjoying the victory of having thrown the communists out of power, and so they would get together and celebrate their victory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This was when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would have been January of 1992. At the same time, the process began of dividing up the assets of the state. And all three parties were in accord that that is what should happen. Let me give you an example -- initially. Let me give you an example. Prior to the outbreak of war, now we're talking about the 2nd of March 1992, this is a month before the war breaks out, there are barricades thrown up in Sarajevo, the Serb side makes certain demands, and the demands are focussed on dividing up the police, dividing up television and so forth. In fact, the SDA was not necessarily opposed to this kind of a division of what up until that time had been a Yugoslav television. For example, Yutel, the Yugoslav television was still functioning in Sarajevo up until May of 1992. All three nationalist parties were objecting to Yutel's coverage of Bosnia because it took a very broad view, it showed things from different perspectives and so forth. My point is, all three of them had a common interest in trying to divide television, communications, assets of municipalities along ethnic lines. The problem was that, of course, they began to argue about who would get what and so forth and so on, and ultimately the Serbs planned to utilise what they had gained to form their own region within Bosnia, and if things worked out, to secede. There is not any contradiction in these various actions that were being taken in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to back up about three months to the Bosnian parliament in October. There was a big debate going on about a memorandum on declaration of the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the -- just to draw your attention to where we are, that was the debate where Karadzic made his famous, what has been termed a threat. At page 77 of your book, you speak of this in some detail, and I'm not going to go very much into this except to ask you this question: Karadzic makes his -- after there's a refusal to refer things to this council of national equality on the grounds that it was not yet in existence, Karadzic then says what he said, and it may be useful just to look at it very quickly. Page 77, he says: "I'm asking you once again, I'm not threatening, but asking you to take seriously the interpretation of the political will of the Serbian people who are represented here by the...", and the quote says SDP, "...and the Serbian renewal movement and a couple of Serbs from other parties. I ask you to take seriously the fact that what you are doing is not good. Is this the road under which you want to direct Bosnia-Herzegovina? The same highway to hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia are travelling? Do not think that you will not lead Bosnia-Herzegovina to hell. And do not think that you will not perhaps lead the Muslim people into annihilation because the Muslim people cannot defend themselves if there is war. How will you prevent everyone from being killed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?" Izetbegovic then responds to that, referring to what Karadzic has said: "His manner and his messages perhaps explain why others also refused to stay in such a Yugoslavia. Nobody else wants the kind of Yugoslavia that Mr. Karadzic wants any more, no one except, perhaps, the Serbian people. Such a Yugoslavia and such a manner of Karadzic are simply hated by the people of Yugoslavia. And I then say to the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina that there will not be war. That is my prediction based on the facts on some confirmed facts. Therefore, sleep peacefully, there is no need to fear because it takes two to tango." It appears almost as if Izetbegovic isn't taking what Karadzic says seriously? Why does he respond in such a way that there will be no war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, in the report, I repeat over and over again that all sides were preparing for war, including the Muslim side in self-defense. This comment by Izetbegovic is meant to reassure as much as anything the international community, if they are listening, that nothing disastrous will happen before Bosnia is recognised as an independent state. On other occasions, in the book we mention how Izetbegovic in seeming contradiction to everything that is going on makes exactly the same kind of statement. Everything is peaceful, everything will be fine. The reason is very simple: He doesn't want the threat of war or fear of war to in any way pose an obstacle to the recognition of Bosnia which he, and I understand him perfectly, feels is the only way they will be saved from a war in which they will be the possible losers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What follows, of course, is a walkout by the Serb deputies that you describe. Later, there's another similar confrontation after the referendum on whether or not there will be a resolution for independence, again the Serbs walk out of parliament.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two major occasions, then, when the Muslims and the Croats basically decide to take positions against the will of the Serbian people, the Serbian delegates at least. My question is this: Do you believe that they knew, the Muslims and the Croats who were taking these positions in the Bosnian parliament, do you think they knew that war would result from that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think that this was their fear, that war would come in any case, and that what they must do was to prepare themselves for this war by trying to gain independence. So they were willing in October to push the issue of the sovereignty of Bosnia as a first step. Then they were going to pick up the ball that Badinter had thrown to them in January of 1992 and prepare a referendum, also for independence, as a second step to lead to recognition of Bosnia. They felt this was the only way that if war came they would be able to defend themselves, if they had already received recognition as an independent state. So these actions are really, although they seem provocative in many ways, a very logical way for them to go if they want to prepare themselves for independence. Mind you, there should have been more intervention on the part of the international community. That's another story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. This brings me back. I'm honestly now feeling a little bit -- to make me feel even more confused, I'm receiving interpretation in Serbo-Croat. Mr. Shoup, please try to make me understand. All this is happening starting October, November, December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: January, and we have the referendum, et cetera. Earlier on, when you had stated that they were enjoying -- the three parties were getting together and celebrating their victory, et cetera, and they asked you to place it within the time frame, you told me January 1992. So what is exactly happening in January 1992? Are they all partying together and celebrating, or are they preparing for war? Because we have heard evidence of what was going on within the Serbian quarters in late 1991, we know or have heard evidence of what was taking place in Sarajevo within the Muslim Bosniak quarters roundabout the same period. I mean, I find it very difficult to understand how you can maintain your position that in January of 1992 everything was so rosy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't, hear, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In January of 1992, they were so pally, I mean, the three parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the case. Let me just state that as a fact. I must say that these people were not unknown to each other. They were -- Mr. Karadzic had been a well-liked psychiatrist in Sarajevo before the war. They knew how to sit down in Yugoslav style and drink a beer together. Let's, however, put this in perspective. There was still hope, I think, that perhaps some way would be found to save either a Yugoslavia through international negotiations of some kind, or to save Bosnia even. I don't think that any of these nationalist parties really were -- how to put it -- ready to just simply for no reason to go to war. They felt compelled to prepare for war. They had completely diametrically opposed agendas, but at the same time they were Bosnians, and they did feel some camaraderie and so forth. This was nothing unusual. They had not yet learned, I think, to hate each other as they would shortly. This is the best I can do to describe that moment that is described in the book. We have quotes in the book which indicate how they sat down to enjoy each other's company briefly in the spring of 1992. That's as far as I can go. Judge, I'm sorry I can't do a better job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I place it in a more particular point -- frame in time. This is just post December 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We know what happened vis-a-vis with regard to Croatia and Slovenia in December of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're saying that they know already about the war in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's the recognition of -- international recognition of both Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think it was obviously clear to everyone also from the evidence that we have heard here that everyone knew that what was going to happen afterwards with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was at that particular moment, December 1991 and January 1992, a little sliver of hope. And this was because an anticipated Serbian offensive against Croatia after she was recognised by the Germans did not take place. Instead, Milosevic actually softened his tone considerably in December of 1991, January of 1992. In December of 1991, he held what he called a convention for the new Yugoslavia. The new Yugoslavia was to be made up of Serbia and Montenegro. He didn't mention the others as members. Two or three months earlier, the official Belgrade position was "we are going to create a Serbia with all of the Serbs in it." Now he said in December, no. He said those Serbs outside of Serbia and Montenegro will have to wait. Now, his calculation might have been that with waiting he would get what he needed anyway. But there was an optimistic mood briefly at that point. And if I might just conclude on this note, it's very interesting. Our Ambassador, Warren Zimmerman, who had been against the recognition of Croatia because he thought it would lead to a rapid spread of the war, now because he saw that Milosevic had softened his tone decided that yes, recognition really works. Let's go ahead and recognise Bosnia, and Milosevic will react in the same way that he reacted to the recognition of Croatia. That's the situation that -- in which these people sit down briefly and enjoy a beer together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other cases, we would have spoken of a comedy of errors. Here, it's a tragedy of errors. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, Professor, we might assist the Judge in understanding this if we would talk about that session on January 25th. That session lasted, according to your book, page 106, until 3.30 in the morning. And that -- this is after the Karadzic speech. It's after the Izetbegovic speech back in October. It's after a lot of things that have happened that don't look good for the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really am sorry but Mr. Ackerman -- each of the questions now is preceded by Mr. Ackerman's summary what he perceives to be the situation to be. This is still a witness. It should just be a question, not Mr. Ackerman's summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the expert witness. Mr. Ackerman should ask him a direct question, and then Professor Shoup can give the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go straight to the question, Mr. Ackerman. I mean, after all, Professor Shoup wrote the book, so he knows exactly what the preceding events, or immediately preceding events were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have been trying to save time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If Ms. Korner doesn't want me to save time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm interrupting you. I shouldn't be interrupting this much, but I'm trying to understand as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court in this marathon session that went on on the 25th of January, were these people at each other's throats or were they trying to come to some kind of an agreed disposition of this issue of independence?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a long quotation, Professor Burg and I, about this session taken from the newspaper Oslobodjenje, which is, of course a -- it's not a Serb newspaper. At this point, it's a quite reliable, independent newspaper. It's a remarkable passage. All of a sudden, these persons who have been provoking each other in various ways seem to come to a point where they realise that they are on the edge of the abyss. The issue is: Should we try to reach some kind of new constitutional arrangements before we declare independence for Bosnia? Because the existing constitutional arrangements are for a unitary state, which of course is totally unacceptable to the Serbs and to the Croatians in Western Herzegovina. Or should we first offer the people of Bosnia a referendum with no reference to constitutional, you know, accommodations for the Serbs and the Croats and then subsequently try to hammer out this question of revising this unitary constitution? I think everyone in that meeting felt that it was necessary to at least address the problem of constitutional reform. You can see even Cengic who was the deputy head of the SDA saying we should address this question of constitutional reform. First, let's say something about it before we issue this referendum. And at this point, late at night, it appears that maybe some progress is being made. The deputies all welcome this suggestion. Izetbegovic stands up and says no. He says we will first submit a referendum with no reference to constitutional reforms. That can be discussed after the declaration of independence has been adopted by the people of Bosnia. It's a remarkable movement. It requires flushing out in the sense that we don't have other accounts than this one. But it's there to show how, I think, the deputies in the assembly were very aware of what was about to happen. They were desperately trying maybe even to accommodate each other, and this fleeting moment then passed. Maybe this interpretation is not correct, but I think it's one that deserved to be put in the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If one look at page 106 at that long quote that you do have from Oslobodjenje, it indicates does it not that at one point in the evening Karadzic and Cengic actually shared the podium, announced they were close to agreement. There was applause from the deputies. And then later on, Izetbegovic made his announcement that there would not be any deal.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot be sure of the sincerity of the actors at this moment. I don't pretend that I know absolutely because at this point the Serbs had already staked out an extreme position about the autonomy of the various autonomous "oglas" that they had formed. It would have been extremely difficult to arrive at some kind of constitutional compromise. Yet the fact remains that at that moment, the only moment that I could ever detect in this long constitutional debate, all three sides seem desperately to be searching for some kind of accommodation before the referendum is voted on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move ahead now to -- I'm going to page 26 of your report. You were talking there about a plan that Milosevic and Tudjman had met and talked about to basically partition Bosnia between Croatia and Serbia. And you say this: If Bosnia was not regarded as having the right to statehood and the history of Bosnia suggested how unprepared she was to undertake this task, then there could be no objection in principle to such a solution." The only question I have about that is what prompts the conclusion that Bosnia was unprepared to undertake the task of statehood?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia was a negative state. It existed as a province of Yugoslavia, part of the Austro-Hungarian empire in a sort of state of arrested development. The ethnic system was one of a very -- almost ancient type. And this was because -- not because the Bosnian state was strong or national consciousness was developed, because no one could agree on how to divide Bosnia up. In other words, she was really a historical residue. Earlier, we commented on the fact that other states surrounding Bosnia had made no -- had no compunctions to an ex-Bosnia, to partition her, whatever the case might be. There was no Bosnian national consciousness; there was -- had never been a Bosnian state since the middle ages; the notion of independence was one in some ways that was shocking; the Muslims themselves had never done more in the past than demand autonomy within Yugoslavia or the independent state of Croatia during World War II. This fact, this historical fact, comes into collusion -- or collision, I should say, with the development of the post communist perception that republics in communist states, however artificial, should remain with their borders intact. Remember, this is something that comes up in the case of the Soviet Union. And so looking at Bosnia, it was natural and not incorrect to say regardless of Bosnia's past, her boundaries must stay where they are or we will be engaged in ethnic conflict and so forth and so on. However, if is it seemed that retaining these boundaries would lead to ethnic conflict, as it did, a civil war, if you agreed that Bosnia had really no great claims for statehood, you might think of other solutions. And there were other solutions that are discussed here in the report and in the book; namely, some kind of a return to the agreement between Croatia and Serbia from 1939. I won't go further than that. But really Bosnia had no, you know, no reason to think that it could just claim independence unless the Muslims were to become the titular nationality, in which case many very difficult issues arose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go to another subject. I'm now up to page 44 of your report. You have a section under the title "ancient hatreds," and you say this: "The notion that the peoples of Bosnia were the prisoners of their violent past enrages the critics of the ancient hatreds theory. However, the fact of the matter was that the families remembered who had engaged in atrocities during World War II and vengeance became the order of the day as regime collapse gathered speed even before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. I do understand that sentence. Here, I talk about vengeance becoming the order of the day. I would, if I had my druthers, Mr. Ackerman, I would rewrite that sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would rewrite it how?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say as Mr. Duijzings said in his very excellent report, vengeance became the order of the day after the atrocities commenced during this current war. Now, there was a tradition of vengeance. This was a cruel society in some respects, and this is why I've included this little account of what happened in Medjugorje as an example of that. But I certainly should not have tried to imply that everybody went out to get even for what they remembered had happened during World War II. I don't want to make that -- I don't want to imply that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is important -- well, I probably shouldn't say this. I'll just ask the question. What role does vengeance play in the Balkan character?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does play a role. In the rural areas of Bosnia and elsewhere, it does play a role. Let me explain. If you live in a small village up in the mountains of Bosnia, or this could be Serbia, could be Macedonia, your whole life is encompassed by the life of the village. And you have a very minute knowledge of not only everybody in the village, but what everybody had done or said or done to another person five years ago, ten years ago, maybe generations ago. That is your life. And this is why oral history is so well developed. An anthropologist who goes to a village in Bosnia or Serbia, as you may know, goes to the individuals, and he will be able to transcribe in great detail a family history and who has done what to whom and so on and so on. And these things then are remembered. Then when violence breaks out for -- ethnic clashes take place and terrible atrocities occur, getting even will happen, you know, in the course of a war. As I said, I think it's extreme -- this is not correct to put it the way I did here, but this is -- these are mountain men, you know. There's nothing remarkable about that. Keep in mind, of course, that the people who were committing the atrocities often even if they were from the neighbourhood were not necessarily themselves the best of the best. They were -- sometimes they were in there for plunder and so forth. Their initial reasons for doing this were not vengeance, but that's -- that cycle began with these kinds of actions. And it led to Srebrenica in 1995, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go now to page 47 of your report under the heading "responsibility for the war." The question I want to ask you, and you lead into it in the first paragraph there, just the last phrase in that paragraph,"what Bosnia was experiencing was indeed a civil war, and that it was precisely this that differentiated the conflict from earlier cases of ethnic violence on Bosnian soil." I do want you to speak for a moment about what you mean by differentiated it from earlier cases of ethnic violence, but I'm also interested in having you explain your conclusion that this was a civil war because this is also an issue of dispute as to whether it was Serbian aggression or in fact a civil war.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I'll try to be brief. These issues, I think, are well known to the Court. But -- wait a minute -- just back, excuse me, to the first question that you posed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had said that it was precisely the civil war aspect that differentiated it from other earlier cases of violence on Bosnian soil.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: In earlier instances the breakdown of law and order had been -- taken place within the context of a world war. Foreign powers were on Bosnian soil. And so the outcome of ethnic conflicts in Bosnia depended on the outcome of the larger war that was being waged on its soil. A war such as World War II. Those wars took their own course, and Bosnia, then, would be under the control of whoever won that war. This was the first time that a truly civil war had arisen in which the three ethnic groups were, in effect, allowed to fight one another until one won or another lost. And this war could have lasted much longer than it did. This was a unique situation. I think the -- some of the observations in the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation point to the fact that most of the wars have not been as destructive or lasted as long because they were not, as my -- as I suggest, purely a civil war between the three ethnic communities. Now, let's go on the second part about a civil war. It seems to me simply that the tensions that were generated in Bosnia, they were-- during the period of the collapse of communism were very real. They created real antagonisms between the three ethnic communities. The Serbs and the Bosnians to simplify had totally different concepts of what the future of Bosnia should be. They mobilised their supporters during this election campaign prior to December 1990 -- 1991, excuse me. All of this is part of the record, and all of this takes place within Bosnia. It is not as though these people, for example, the SDS, the Serbian party, is being paid and funded and urged and created by Belgrade. And I state here if it can be shown, and maybe I'm wrong, but it could be shown that Karadzic's party was simply a creation of Belgrade and all of these events that led to this confrontation before the war even broke out were simply the result of the manoeuvres of outside powers, then I would perhaps be willing to acknowledge that this was aggression. But otherwise, since this was -- these tensions were -- originated from within Bosnia itself, I can't accept that. I won't go further into the war itself. There were so many instances in which Belgrade and Pale were, you know, in conflict with another. You could see it's not just the case of a puppet relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that raises an interesting question. And I don't know if you know the answer to it or not. The HDZ, the Croat party in Bosnia, was the counterpart of the same party in Croatia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, if you know, why was not there a counterpart of Milosevic's party in Bosnia instead of a totally separate SDS?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was one of the objections raised by a reviewer of the book who said that we don't explain why -- why Milosevic simply didn't form his own party. To me, the answer is because these processes were going forward in Bosnia on their own and had deep roots in Bosnia itself, whereas the Croatian case was one where Belgrade had a greater role in actually influencing the direction which the Serb movement was going. And by the way, there was a moderate, Vareskovic, in Croatia who was in effect forced out of power by the machinations in Belgrade. This didn't happen in Bosnia. But I can't explain why Milosevic didn't do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of quote in your report on page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know why I turn on my microphone. I speak too fast anyhow. It might be better for the interpreters if I left it off. You have quote from Professor Robert Hayden on page 49. I think before we refer to it, you should tell the Chamber who he was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Robert Hayden is an expert, again, on Yugoslavia. He is a professor at the University of Pittsburgh. He is a trained anthropologist and legal specialist, and he has testified actually in front of the Tribunal on earlier occasions. I believe, I am not certain of this, maybe as a Defence expert witness in the Tadic case. Some of you may know for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're on the topic, this, if you look at the footnote, this refers to an unpublished manuscript by this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if the professor has this unpublished manuscript with him which he can supply to us so we can have a look at it because he's apparently relying on this quote, and because it's unpublished we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand your concern. And I was told just before I left that the Court would need this document. Unfortunately, I didn't have time to bring it with me. I have then sent an email to Professor Hayden to email it to the Court. I don't think we've gotten a copy from him yet, have we? I can telephone him perhaps and he can send it to you. I have a copy at home, but I just couldn't find it in time to bring it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The request was made to email it to me and it hadn't come yet. I don't know whether that's because he's out of town and not getting his emails or what.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour will recall, I raised this a considerable time ago, and said that if an expert was going to rely on unpublished material it should be supplied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll make every effort to bring it. I thought it would come -- I thought that Professor Hayden would supply us with it, but I'll have to phone him and find out why it hasn't come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I made the request immediately after Ms. Korner raised it, and it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has confirmed that. But we still don't have it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer is we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your quote from Professor Hayden, however, says this: "Political deadlock in this case meant that the Bosnian State failed. The organised political authority lost the allegiance of at least half of the population and also lost control over the territories that the people who rejected it controlled. Of course, it is often true in any civil war that the government loses the allegiance of some citizens and control over some territories, but the difference in Bosnia was the internationally recognised government never had either the allegiance of half its putative citizens or control over even half of its supposed territory to begin with. Indeed, Bosnian independence was recognised by the international community not because the people of Bosnia wanted it, but rather precisely because so many of them did not. Thus, Bosnia manifested what might be termed negative sovereignty, external insistence that it be one country when half of its own population was determined to divide it." What's your reaction to that quote?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate that this may need explanation. And if I did it again, I would provide it right in the report. This seems to contradict the results of the referendum that took place in -- at the end of February because in the referendum which asked the peoples of Bosnia did they wish independence, some 64 per cent of the population, as you know, said yes, we want independence. What Professor Hayden is referring to is the problem of the Croatian vote. And this is explained in my report, I believe, in more detail in the book. The Croatian vote is deceptive. They voted for independence of Bosnia, but a certain segment of that vote was not actually for the independence of Bosnia but for dividing Bosnia up. Why would they vote for the independence of Bosnia? Because at that particular moment, it was of overriding importance to Zagreb that the integrity of Bosnia be defended because the integrity of Croatia was threatened. And so he made it very clear to the Bosnian Croatians they should vote for independence. You will notice if you've read our book that it wasn't long afterwards that the leader of the HDZ party of the Croatian party sat down, Mate Boban, with Karadzic at Grac and agreed to partition Bosnia. So what Professor Hayden is relating to is the fact that a large number of Croatians, plus the Serbs, were really, in fact, determined to partition Bosnia, even though the results of the referendum didn't reflect that fact. This is not a disputable fact. The results of the referendum are very deceiving. They don't really reflect what the Croatians of Bosnia wanted. The question is, how many Croatians? And here, Professor Hayden may be pushing things a little bit because there were Croatians living in Sarajevo or living in Central Bosnia who genuinely and sincerely wished Bosnia to remain as an independent state. They voted in the referendum without any other motives in mind. And I say in the footnote if you wanted to calculate carefully the secessionist Croatians and then take the Serbian vote together, you would probably get 40 to 45 per cent of the vote. Still, this is practically half of the people of Bosnia who, in fact, did not want Bosnia to declare its independence who were for some form of partitioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move forward now and change subjects again. During the war, and I'm mostly focussing on 1992, but looking at the war as a whole, there are a number of exhibits and materials that discuss this issue. And I don't want to simply sit here and read all those documents to the Court because the Court can read them. But I would like you to just discuss generally the relationship between the SDS and the VRS. What was that relationship, did it change as the war went on? That sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I'll try to be brief. That problem of the relationship between the political side of the Serbian independence movement and the VRS, which is the Vojska Republike Srpska, or the Serbian Army, is not something that we dealt with, Professor Burg and I, in great detail in the book. We were not really experts on this particular point. However, in the book you will see something very striking, and that is that by the end of the war, General Mladic, with the support of his officers, I presume, and Karadzic had completely split. Karadzic had fired Mladic actually as leader of the VRS, and Mladic had continued to be close to Belgrade and was operating on his own at that particular point. So the political and the military relationship on the Serb side was extremely strained. You will get a great deal of insight into that relationship in the documents provided by the Defence and in the CIA reports ""Balkan Battlegrounds"" where you will see that the military was very resentful of the meddling of the politicians in purely military affairs. And the civilian side, the SDS, was also very corrupt, and this was something that the military, too, found very difficult to accept. I won't go any further, just except to point out those strains. They were constant apparently. We learn more and more about them all the time. I would simply conclude by saying that those strains climaxed with the Srebrenica massacre of 1995. Because it does appear that the military, Mladic, had military motives for carrying out that massacre. And whether Karadzic himself would have approved this or not, I'm not privy to the material that has been unfolding here in the Court and I won't even try to assume one thing or another. But I think it's important to see that that continuing tension carries over into the situation that occurred in July of 1995. It's very, very tantalising to know more, but I don't want to go further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the VRS was formed and General Mladic took control of the VRS, do you know what his attitude was toward paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was very scornful of them. We have a good deal of evidence again from these new publications that I am constantly referring to, that the generals within the VRS tried to bring these paramilitaries under their control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at Exhibit DB371, at page 266, the CIA report has this to say: "Bosnian Serb President Karadzic --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I just -- are we ""Balkan Battlegrounds"" now or what? One or two?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. ""Balkan Battlegrounds" Two", page 266, Ms. Korner. But it's also Exhibit DB371.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 371, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might just say for the record that "Balkan Battlegrounds, Volume II" is not yet generally available. No one seems to be able to get it except for Professor Shoup who must have some incredible connections with the CIA because he has got it and none of the rest of us can get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event: "Bosnian Serb President Karadzic..." -- I'm quoting "...formalised the main staff's efforts to eliminate rogue elements with the proclamation of a decree on 13 June 1992 prohibiting the formation and operation of armed groups and individuals not under the unified command of the armed forces or the police force." This is the -- you had talked about Karadzic trying to fire Mladic later on in 1995.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm, mm-hm. Earlier, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It appears that in June of 1992, he's trying to help him by eliminating the paramilitaries --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think there's any difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, may I ask who is the author of these very straight lines, underlines, page 266 in particular and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am the author of that. And not to interrupt. This was my personal acquisition, and I simply went to work on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We tried to get another copy of "Balkan Battlegrounds", Your Honour. It was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure it is actually --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All of the underlining and the arrows and everything in are Professor Shoup's that took place in Virginia before he ever made it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope this is not going to expose the witness to any kind of trouble for making use, public use of this document. It's not classified or anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, it's not a secret document. It's just not available in the government printing office yet, and as a result, no one else seems to be able to get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if that is the case, we will --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe by today, it is on the website. But it wasn't there last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Or earlier in this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to protect the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think there's any problem with that at all, is there, Professor Shoup?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want -- I'm skipping some material here because, as I said, it makes no sense to sit here and read these things to the Judges when they can read them themselves, but I am interested in this issue about paramilitaries. If we look over at page 286 into the footnotes, there's a description there of an interview with Lieutenant General Milan Gvero, who apparently was close to the top of that VRS chain of command. It says Mladic, Gvero, and many other ex-JNA officers had an abhorrence for a disunited command, as Gvero implies, and constantly enforced the VRS prerogatives as the sole RS armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 286, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Assuming operational control over all MUP units in combat. They hardly despised the volunteers and paramilitaries, and particularly deplored their penchant for looting rather than fighting." In a 1993 interview, then Major General Slavko Lisica described his dislike for volunteers stating: "These were not fighters, but rather adventurers and the usual dregs that every war brings to the surface. They are disorganised, irresponsible, and have never fit in with my concept of combat. You have guys who will kill a 90-year-old man just for a lamb. They ask me to send them out for so-called cleansing. Okay, I say. There are some minefields you can clear out to your heart's content. Volunteers have been a burden in my zone of responsibility so that on one occasion I even sent in tanks to disarm them." Did that problem ever change? Were the paramilitaries active throughout the war, or did Mladic succeed in getting a unified command together, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you what I do know. It won't be a complete answer. There were some paramilitaries under the command of the Red Berets and the Ministry of the Interior in Serbia, and they continued to operate independently of the VRS I think right along to the end of the war. So they are, however, under somebody's command. They are not operating completely independently. I think I could probably find examples of paramilitary forces that operated completely on their own after 1992, but not many. There were paramilitary forces integrated into the VRS, and they would often take on the most difficult assignments, which is somewhat in contradiction to what you just read because they would, sometimes, be better fighters than the ordinary conscript. And so on the front lines of Sarajevo, you could encounter these paramilitary groups dressed up in their colourful uniforms and so forth. They were simply part of the operational VRS army. So I assume they were under their commands. If you're talking about a paramilitary force operating completely on its own after 1992, with the exception maybe of the Yellow Wasps in Eastern Bosnia, I can't -- I must say I don't think there were many of them, if any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at DB373, this is annex 27 to the CIA volume two document. It begins at page 303. I know you're familiar with this particular section, Professor Shoup. It's the section of the report that really deals very specifically with the Bosnian Serb takeover in April of 1992. It speaks of what has been a lot of the evidence in this Court. It talks about Kljuc, it talks about Prijedor. It talks about Sanski Most. And it talks about ethnic cleansing and sets that out in some detail. The only part of that that I want to bring to your attention and have you comment on, because the rest of it is quite well-known to this Trial Chamber, is the last paragraph on page 306 which the CIA report calls "the final analysis." And again, I was speaking too fast. Page 306, the report says this: "The Bosnian Serb Army undertook these ethnic cleansing operations because it believed the Muslim population posed an armed threat or could act as a fifth column during the war with the Bosnian government. The VRS focussed on seizing weapons from the population and on detaining military-aged males supports this analysis, that the Bosnian Serb's paranoia greatly exaggerated this supposed threat does not mean that the VRS did not believe it. The few armed Muslim groups that managed to form and survive the Serb assaults and make sporadic guerrilla attacks on VRS and MUP forces in the region inflamed this paranoia still further". Setting aside a quarrel that we might have with the use of the language there, what comment can you make that might help us understand that a little better.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me take a step backward. We have spoken already of the fact that there was tension between the politicalness and the military side of the Serb movement during the war. I'm not sure that we mentioned that General Mladic and other officers were brought up in what can be loosely called the partisan tradition. That tradition did not lend itself to, let's say, ethnic cleansing for the sake of ethnic cleansing. So it has been a puzzle to me why the VRS would engage in ethnic cleansing operations, as this report clearly shows, when many of the leading officers really had not been raised to treat civilians, Muslims, or whoever in this very brutal fashion. This provides the first evidence that I have seen, providing that I believe the CIA's competence here, that the VRS was really -- had a military objective in participating in that ethnic cleansing. Let me give you some proof of that. If you look at other parts of Bosnia, you will find that exactly the same tactics were being used, and my guess is they did have -- not a guess, but my knowledge is they had a military component. Let me give you the example of the town of Tarcin, which you perhaps know, T-a-r-c-i-n, south of Sarajevo. This is one of the towns that struck me in my research because Serbs were all rounded up and pressed into a silo where they were kept for the duration of the war in very abysmal conditions. It sounded very much like just what was happening here in parts of northern Bosnia to the Muslims. Then I realised that there was a strategic reason for this. This was a vital part of the Muslim front, the place where the Muslim front from the south touched on Sarajevo. And so they had cleaned out the civilian population to assure the security of that area. And my guess is with further investigation, you would find the Croatians doing the same thing in Kupres or the Muslims doing the same thing in other places. In other words, this is something that happened all over Bosnia. Now, having said that, there are -- here's an account in which there is brutality. The particular example that is given here of a village involves persuading the peasants, deceiving them to go out and then they are being shot. Just simply -- the women, children are being thrown into a ditch. If the VRS is doing that, then I don't understand. This is seemingly in contradiction to what we read right here. But might I end with a little anecdote to illustrate the role of civilians in this war because this is a true story of a student of mine who was from Bosnia. At the time of the siege of Tuzla by the Serb forces, he had relatives on -- who were inside the city of Tuzla, and he had relatives, Serbs, who were outside bombarding the city. The Serbs who were outside the city telephoned his father in United States who in turn telephoned his relatives inside the city of Tuzla, and the people who were bombarding the city then asked him, how did we do? And then the man telephoned his friends inside Tuzla to find out where the shots had landed, and then telephoned them back where they were in the village to tell them how accurate their artillery was. It sounds bizarre, but in effect it shows you the difficulties in separating the civilian from the military actions in this civil war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back now, and this relates, I think, to your earlier testimony about civil war and the civil war versus the internationality of this conflict. Page 275 in DB371A, the CIA makes this conclusion. It's in the right-hand column just under "help from Big Brother." "Among the many misconceptions about the VJ," that would be the JNA, "VRS relationship, most striking is that large numbers of Yugoslav Army ground troops fought in Bosnia during the conflict and that the VRS was under the command JNA/VJ general staff. There is no evidence to support this notion despite frequent assertions by ill-informed journalists." Does that support your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That supports what I know about the situation. I'm very interested to see that the CIA was -- exhaustively studied this problem comes to this conclusion. They can trace where every unit was during the entire war. I don't know how they did it. Aerial surveillance or something. The whole two volumes are just filled with these charts to show you where each part of the army was. So this is certainly correct. Let me not dwell on that except to give you another example. In our volume we say that in the early years of the war, in 1992, when the Bosnian Serbs were cut off from Serbia because the corridor between Banja Luka to the west and Bijeljina and Serbia to the east had been cut by Croatian and Muslim forces, that an offensive to retake the corridor was launched by the Serbs. This was a desperate effort because they were completely isolated in Western Bosnia. We write that this had to have been done with the assistance of the JNA -- with the JNA -- it was no longer the JNA but... we couldn't conceive of how they could operate that successfully. The CIA says the Serb armies did it all themselves, with no help from Belgrade whatsoever. I was astounded when I read that because it was so vitally important for the Serb cause. And this raised my suspicions as always that Belgrade's attitude towards Bosnia was always very manipulative and always looking at their own self-interests first for one reason or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to do another subject change now. I'm now going to start referring to some of the materials from the Netherlands Institute of War Documentation. Before I do that, I want to know if you have had occasion to look over those materials at some length; and second, if so, give the Court your impression of the value of those materials, the scholarship that went into them, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not read all of that report. It is immense, as you know. And many of you who have looked at can appreciate that. I find it a breakthrough in our knowledge of the Bosnian situation. They summarise things beautifully. They go into details. They seem to have unlimited resources, you know, to track things down. And I consider that to be the most authoritative and the most informative research on Bosnia bar none. I'm gratified to see that the things that Professor Burg and I wrote seemed to have been more or less confirmed, but we certainly didn't go into as much detail as they did. And I would in particular recommend to the Court the Appendix 4 by Ger Duijzings, Professor Duijzings, the anthropologist, who goes into Eastern Bosnia and reconstructs everything that happened there from before the war and through the war itself in immense detail showing exactly how these politicians and local people were relating to one another. It is fascinating. Absolutely fascinating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a section near the beginning -- it's actually in Appendix 5 of the report, however, near the beginning of that appendix. It's in DB361 on the second page of that exhibit. And the subject matter I want to discuss now has to do with the economy and what happened to the economy in Yugoslavia and thus in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between 1980 and 1991. This report from the Netherlands Institute speaks about -- the first of that paragraph talks about the Netherlands itself being one of the oldest and most stable constitutional states in the world, and one of the least violent, very little murder, very few crimes of violence. But then says this: "If within a period of ten years, the economy were to collapse almost completely, the central government became incapable of maintaining law and order, the state disintegrated and power devolved into the hands of local potentates who openly encouraged the use of force. In other words, if the same were to happen in the Netherlands as happened in Yugoslavia from 1980 to 1991 could we be so sure that no Serbian-type events would take place there." This seems to indicate a really fairly dramatic downturn --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're off again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ask the expert a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll stop. You can stop objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what happened in the economy -- tell the Chamber about what happened in the economy in Yugoslavia from 1980 to 1991. What happened?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief again. The Yugoslavia economy was in a state of rapid decline throughout the whole decade of the 1980s. I won't go into the details. Susan Woodward whom -- whose face I didn't know yesterday wrote extensively and very brilliantly on the problems of the economic decline of Yugoslavia in the 1980s. The problem was much more severe in a republic like Bosnia than in a republic like Slovenia with its firm contacts with Austria or with Italy. I have talked to Bosnians who remember how their contacts abroad were cut off. For example, they had a very thriving industry of selling furniture to the United States, which was, of course, appropriate for Bosnia. Well, with these economic difficulties and then the early crisis, those contacts were completely cut off. Their heavy industries were inappropriate to a reformed economy. They didn't make money. And so they began to layoff workers massively as well. This economy in Bosnia was geared towards war industries and some extraction industries of course. Finally, in 1991 Milosevic imposed an embargo or sanctions against Bosnia-Herzegovina, economic sanctions. Why? Because Izetbegovic, acting, as I said earlier, as the government almost of Bosnia had decided he would remain neutral in the war in Croatia, and Milosevic was going to punish him, and this is what he did. And you can imagine this was a sort of final blow for this economy, all of its foreign contacts being cut off. Maybe not completely all of them. A crisis in the Yugoslav economy and then on top of that economic sanctions. It was a time of severe economic crisis in the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If these economic ties were cut off with Serbia by Milosevic's actions and with Zagreb by the fact that there's a war going on in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what effect would that have had on the Krajina area that we're primarily interested in here?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I won't speculate whether it would have more or less effect, let's say, than in other parts of Bosnia. I just can't say really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is very happy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go now to -- it's again DB361. Netherlands Institute materials, page 3, about halfway down, they're talking about the effect of television, but there's a part there that I'm interested in because it refers to this economic situation. "Television had an almost hypnotic effect. This was particularly so in Serbia." And then this: "Where the population became too poor to buy newspapers."

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Absolutely. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That strikes me as amazing that people couldn't afford newspapers. Do you think that happened all over Yugoslavia, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, yes. Let me give you an example from today's Herald Tribune if any of you have read it, it talks about a Russian peasant situated outside of Moscow who is living alone in his little hut. He's over 70 years old. Everybody has deserted him. He can hardly find firewood to keep himself warm, and the only thing he has left is his television set. And he watches Brazilian soap operas the whole day long. I mean, this is so sad. And yet it does reflect what has happened, you know, in places where people have been destitute or suffering economic difficulties. All they have left is their television set.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go now to the next document in the Netherlands Institute materials. It's DB362. And it's page 9 of a section, but it's the only page, I believe, that I have reproduced. And I'm interested in just one sentence. "The population..." -- this is referring to the population of Yugoslavia basically -- "The population was never given the opportunity of properly coming to terms with the tragic events that occurred between 1941 and 1945." What is meant by, if you know, "never given the opportunity of properly coming to terms" with these events?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just briefly that of course during the communist period there was no serious analysis by the historians or otherwise of what had really happened in Yugoslavia. You would find, and if you read Politika or you read Borba during these periods, there would be articles interspersed of how the partisans had done this or that. But basically I can testify from my own experience, people remembered what had happened within their own experience or that of their families. But nothing else really. Tremendously great ignorance. Now, I won't say that's true of Slovenia, perhaps. There were differences there. They had newspapers from abroad and so on. But certainly in Serbia, this was true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Serbia or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Serbia, yeah. In Belgrade, after all, which was flooded with all kinds of foreigners, and so on. But can I just make one more remark. I would warn the Court that just from our western point of view, the idea that knowledge is somehow going to provide a better and more informed way of looking at things doesn't necessarily hold true. I have had long, long discussions over many, many years as they say trying to straighten out the crooked Drina River, and I've never succeeded. So all of my input went basically in vain and whether a lot of enlightened information would have penetrated what were basically very ethnically rooted positions on what happened in World War II, I'm rather dubious. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Appropriate moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you, Professor Shoup. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before we proceed, Mr. Ackerman, I have been asked by the witness to inform you that he, himself, will call Professor Hayden and ask him to email you or to send you the document, so I don't suppose you have to trouble yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's preferable, Your Honour, as Professor Shoup's in the middle of evidence, that it's Mr. Ackerman who reminds Professor Hayden that he's supposed to be providing his unpublished --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just being an ambassador. I'm just saying -- I expected a reaction either you from or Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I haven't the first idea how to reach Professor Hayden, Your Honour. None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you're able to finish today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste more time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had spoken to us earlier about the -- when the nationalist parties took over, this whole concept of carving up Bosnia. There's a couple of references to that I want to refer you to. I'm looking now at DB366. This is from the Netherlands Institute report. I'm at page number 8. This is talking about a September 1990 SDA meeting in Nova Kasaba. And at the top of that page 8, the following language appears: "Nonetheless, the meeting highlighted what was perhaps the most important issue at stake in the elections, both for the SDA and the SDS, control over the local economy. The SDA representative from Zvornik complained that all the income generated by the local aluminum plant, Benicia, went to Serbia. He promised that the first thing he would do after winning the elections was to bring the company under his control so he could start financing the arms needed to fight the Serbs." Now, I take it that's an example of what you were talking about, about the effort to take control over the assets of the various municipalities' economies. Am I correct or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's still a leading question, and I renew my objection to all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your objection is sustained, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going back to the documents. What, may I ask, has what happened in Benicia got to do with the autonomous region of Krajina. This gentleman knows nothing about the autonomous region of Krajina. He made absolutely clear. What Your Honours are dealing with are -- is the events in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I understand the general background that Mr. Ackerman is asking Professor Shoup to give, but this is specifics. Now, Your Honour, I do say this is irrelevant. I'm going to at the end of this renew my objection to the admission of any of these documents. But for the moment, I cannot see how this can be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there was another part to it. Mr. Ackerman will understand what I am going to say, that this statement attributed to Mr. -- whoever it is, the SDA representative from Zvornik, does not mention only the taking over or control of this company as part of what you have suggested to be in line with what the witness said. But also, as being a means to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So just read that paragraph and rephrase your question completely. But do take into account what I have said and what Ms. Korner has objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I really need to respond to that objection because in my view it's not well taken at all. Nothing happened in Bosnia in a vacuum in 1992. People in Banja Luka knew what was happening in Srebrenica, people in Srebrenica knew what was happening in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a statement you are making, Mr. Ackerman, which could be founded or it could also be a gratuitous one. And I will not comment on that. But I would rather prefer that you restricted yourself to the statement which we will accept, of course, that nothing happened in a vacuum, neither in Bosnia, in the Krajina, nor elsewhere. Anyway, shall we skip this and go to the next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is this, Professor: Did the events that were happening in Bosnia in 1991 or 1992 happen in a vacuum, or did things that happened in Western Bosnia become known in the Krajina and things that happened in the Krajina become known in Western Bosnia? In other words, was there communication throughout the country? Was the telephone service working, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, the telephone service was working. People would be informing each other of what was going on. I think that a much more important point to make is that such incidents as this one were rapidly transmitted to the Belgrade press which then rapidly transmitted it back into all of Serbia. In other words, much of the information, as I say in my report, that people were receiving at this point was from sources outside of Bosnia itself. And the Serbian press would be very quick to pick up on anything that would, you know, seed distrust or anxiety among the Serb population. I don't know if they did in this particular instance, but this is a classic case of the kind of thing that would appear in Vecene Novoste the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Only that the people were too poor to afford buying the papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't stop people from buying the paper and passing on the information to others, especially in a city like Banja Luka which is of course full of newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really quite hesitant about this presentation because I'm starting to have the feeling the Court is absolutely disinterested in the history of what went on during this conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't stopped you, Mr. Ackerman. I haven't stopped you. But you all realise that I can quite understand and I accept first and foremost, even before everyone else, I suppose, that what happened in Bosnia did not happen in a vacuum. But that's not the beginning and the end of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber or at least Your Honour seemed quite sympathetic to the objection that what happened in Western Bosnia has nothing to do with the Krajina, and I think that's not true. I think it has a great deal to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did not say that. Don't attribute to me what I didn't say. I never said that. Go to the transcript and see what I said. I said that the objection that Ms. Korner was raising so far as it was an objection directed to the question as such and the way it was put was a valid one, and I was accepting the objection, sustaining the objection. And I also pointed out to you that although your question was referring to only one part of -- or was referring to one part only of what the witness had stated earlier, there was a second element to the statement of this gentleman, the SDA representative from Zvornik. And you could not possibly in one question separate the one from the other. Your question was directed to the previous statement of the expert that the Serbs and the Muslims were more interested in sharing the spoils or grabbing what was there to grab. But at no time did the witness mention that this was being done with the ulterior motive that this gentleman from Zvornik specifically refers to. So I hope you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So go ahead. And I'm not putting any restraints on you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I remain interested in the economic aspects of what was happening, and I want to now refer you to another section which we find. It's DB369, Appendix 4, final remarks, it's called. And it's about halfway down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's page 3 of DB369.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Duijzings is now sort of summing up and making his final remarks in this book that he basically has written. He talks about the dramatic economic and political crisis of the 1980s after Tito's death and the ways these affected the situation on the ground in a small area such as Srebrenica. And then he says this: "In all practical terms, the economic crisis was dramatic. Reducing salaries to a fraction of what they were only a decade earlier, and leaving people unemployed and deeply insecure about their existence and future. From the Serb perspective, the economic crisis was exacerbated by the threat of political marginalisation resulting from the demographic growth and social and political emancipation of the Bosnian Muslim nation. Local Serbs were highly susceptible to propaganda from Belgrade which subsumed all these processes under the label Islamic fundamentalism. However, it was the fight over the economic assets in times of uncertainty and economic crisis which formed the crucial background to many of the conflicts. History was a symbolic resource retrieved from nationalist folklore. It was the most effective tool in mobilising the population." Now, my question is this: Duijzings is talking there about what effect these things had on Srebrenica. From your research and reading, was this a Bosnia-wide effect? Did it affect all of Bosnia-Herzegovina in much this way?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- let me say broadly I agree completely with Professor Duijzings's conclusions, which I think are very balanced and which apply to all of Bosnia, especially because he does not pinpoint anything peculiar to the Eastern Bosnian situation so much as talking about broad-based problems, the economic crisis, the possible political marginalisation of the Serbs, fear of Islamic fundamentalism in which history is a symbolic resource, all of these things apply to a Bosnia which is in extreme, extreme distress. And I must say really frankly, I'm not surprised that everyone took this attitude of, sort of, "sauve qui peut," save yourself. I don't see anything very strange about it. It was cloaked in nationalist rhetoric, and it had many very dangerous people taking advantage of that situation. But I think there's just no question, and these are the elements. I would maybe juggle them a little bit differently. But the crisis was profound. Might I just say a word or two more on that while you search for your document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, go right ahead.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One thing that I have -- I think that can be overlooked is that after the elections of December 1991, Bosnia was simply not the same place. It had enjoyed a cultural -- multiculturalism and even multiethnicity that had never threatened to spill over into the realm of real power because the party held it. Now, after 1991, 110 different municipalities are all trying to grab power for themselves. The outcome is a disaster. My own opinion, and that's -- but I can state an opinion because I've thought about this for a very long time, is that sooner or later Bosnia would have lost her earlier multiethnic character and national regions would have emerged which would have, even within a Bosnian state, had to come to terms with each other. This was the inevitable outcome of this terrible disaster that -- the disappearance of the old Bosnia, which we all loved very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Duijzings finally concludes this way, page 4 of DB363, speaking about his approach to this topic: "My approach is based on the fundamental presumption that people make history in two related ways: One, by imagining and constructing a past which is relevant for the present; and two, by the way they choose to act, taking among other things their visions of the past into account. It underscores that history is the work of people who act and interact with different motives and interests in mind, the chemistry of which leads to results which are often unintended in their final outcome." Do you agree with this approach?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think this is what has informed the research that I have undertaken, having known both -- all sides of this problem. And I would simply say that that research is sometimes misunderstood as being too tolerant of one side or the other. It's not true. I think Professor Duijzings' accomplishment here is to show that you can uncover this beast, you can look at every side of this issue, as he has done in depth, in amazing depth, and really come out with this kind of very nuanced understanding. I'm enthusiastic about this conclusion. I think it should be something that should be in print rather than hidden in electronic form someplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, I want to look for just a moment at DB370 and page 3 of that document. "Though it is generally agreed" - this is the last paragraph on that page - "that a knowledge of history is important for a proper understanding of the background to the Yugoslav conflict, it is very difficult to explain the wars solely on the basis of historical analogies without taking the recent power struggle between the political elites into account. It is clear, however, that the various parties have misused history to justify their aggressive policies towards other ethnic groups and to cloak the real political objectives which generally involve boundary changes at the expense of their neighbours." I think you can elaborate on that just a bit.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, these are the very considered conclusions of a group of researchers who have done a magnificent job at the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation. I find it, again, a very, very profound and very careful statement of the case. I would, however, like to remind the Court that underlying the clash between these various power elites is the national question. How should states be formed? Should an area be permitted to secede and join another state, or should it not? This has been the problem that faced Yugoslavia and tore her apart, and this was the problem in Bosnia. It was a profound difference in the view of the Serbian leadership, if -- you can call them extreme if you wish, but they believed this, that their portions of Bosnia should have the right to secede and to join the "matica", the motherland. The Bosnians had this profound feeling that the boundaries of Bosnia were sacrosanct, that they would be able to live in that Bosnia with the Serbs and Croatians. Ultimately, they would become the titular nationality. These were the fundamental issues that tore Bosnia apart. Maybe there was selfishness and ambition and misuse of history on all sides, but the underlying goals of these groups were clearly best understood in terms that I've tried to put them forth to you now, that is profound disagreements over the state of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This quote concludes with that language "to cloak the real political objectives which generally involve boundary changes at the expense of their neighbours." One of the questions that intrigues me is: Was there a difference between objectives that people at the top in leadership might have from those that a soldier on the ground in Bosnia might have? I mean, is there any indication that those objectives passed all the way down to people on the ground, or were they pursuing different objectives at times?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an interesting question. You will pardon the pause, but part of the answer, Mr. Ackerman, is right here in the book. Chapter 4, the war on the ground, you certainly know that concluding passage here, or almost-concluding passage, by the officer Milovan Stankovic. With your permission, I would just like to read his quotation, one paragraph. It won't take long. That's page 185. "Our policy has never. "... And so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Here is a man who may be discouraged." It's 1994, and he speaks bluntly. "Our policy has never defined the basic aims of the struggle. Political or national or economic or regional aims. It has never been stated of what state it is, of what size, and what cities are to be taken. The policy says that the border is as far as the army boot can reach. To say the least, frivolous, a boot can easily slip. When we took Doboj during the first days of the war we formed" and so forth. I won't go any further. And look over -- what he says over here on the next page, the second paragraph on page 186. It is one of the most illuminating statements that we found in our research. He says: "Military defeat is a coverup for policy. What? I will give you one example that staggered me.
