I said that out of our common interests, we should hand over some territories to the enemy, but let it be after the war and only under condition that our people are compensated. One people's deputy, I will not name him, says to me that do you think that that is the -- in the interest of the state for a man to wait until the end of the war and then to give him with a committee and say his house is worth 150.000 German marks. It works out much better if he moves out" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. We cannot follow you at this speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Do you think that it is in the interests of the state for a man to wait until the end of the war and then you have to give him with a committee and say that his house is worth 150 thousand German marks. It works out much better if he moves out with only his shirt on his back. Then he will be happy with whatever he gets in the end. I cannot reconcile myself to such games." It's a profoundly revealing of the problems that were facing the Karadzic regime at that point in the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I have one final question: One of the things I asked you to do was to consult your library and look at the major published works, published books about the events in Yugoslavia from 1991 to 1995 to see if you found Brdjanin's name in any of those publications. Did you perform that task?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that. I searched all my own personal library, which is extensive. I didn't find Brdjanin's name in the index of one of the books that I searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Will you finish in five minutes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course. But I wouldn't mind asking a few preliminary questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. You have five minutes. I won't deprive you. Cross-examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, do you know who Radoslav Brdjanin is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't understand you, please. More slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has become part of the interpreters' team now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Radoslav Brdjanin is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the crisis committee of the ARK and served in various posts before he became -- before he became -- not president, vice-president of the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as your library contains absolutely no reference to him in any book, how did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only found it out through the materials that I was sent and that I've used here. Frankly, I can't remember when that precise knowledge came to me. But I think it was probably only after I got here. Mind you, I could have found it out other ways because your point is well taken. If I had wanted to, I'm sure I would have found his exact position by going into LexisNexis, for example, and reading some of the dispatches from BBC and so on from earlier times. I didn't bother to do that. But certainly, you're correct, I could have found out what his position was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever read the indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you haven't any idea what Mr. Brdjanin did, apart from his positions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I would object that the indictment describes anything Mr. Brdjanin did. It's a bunch of allegations that they have to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't describe anything he did, and I suggest that he didn't do any of those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, just rephrase your -- that part of your question, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know, Professor, what the allegations are against Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I certainly do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know what the evidence in this case has been?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. Wait a minute, I take that back. I have read Mr. Donia's -- some of the testimony of Professor Donia. In the course of that testimony, Mr. Brdjanin's name arises on occasion. I can tell you that much, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever met Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, I've never met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can do that, Professor Shoup, can you tell us, please, this Court, what is the purpose of the evidence that you have been giving for the last day or two days, if you include the film?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's extremely important to make a point, and that is that Bosnia had become a totally dysfunctional place after the elections of 1991. As I said earlier, people were trying to respond to this situation to get by as best they could. And that the Serbs in turn were taking actions which were viewed as being somehow aggressive or somehow inexplicable, but they were not in that context. I don't approve of them. I think they went the wrong direction. But the context shows that their response was not surprising, and secondly, in respect to things such as ethnic cleansing and so forth, that these things were happening on the other side as well, to what extent more or less we can talk about if you wish to pursue that subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there are two things that arise out of that answer. The first is this: You are not trying to suggest, are you, that because Bosnia was dysfunctional that, therefore, excuses the commission of war crimes by individuals?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to suggest that war crimes must be sifted through a Balkan situation and not for us to stand off and try to apply standards and imagine the Bosnian situation as one that we're more comfortable with, that is, one that is not as complicated and so on. I think that's what was done during the war itself. We had to talk about a war of aggression because we felt more comfortable with it. No, there were bad people on all sides. Until we can come to terms with that and the Court can act in that context, I would be very upset. And I think we've made a great deal of progress today in providing a background by which the Judges can make that kind of judgement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do I understand you to say you are saying that the dysfunction in Bosnia, the Balkan situation, does excuse the commission of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not. I'm saying quite the opposite. I am saying that there were war crimes committed that you might not even have known about. I have a whole section in my report which you perfectly well know about victimisation and strategies of victimisation, and nobody, to the best of my knowledge, and I apologise to the Court if I'm wrong, has considered the horrible crimes that were committed by people firing on their own civilians. I have seen no sign of anyone --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, you're becoming rather excited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this is becoming impossible for the interpreters. I really sympathise with you, and I apologise myself. This must be terrible for you. So I think we need to stop here, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one last point, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We call it a day after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, can I explain to you, which clearly was not explained to you by Mr. Ackerman, this Court is not here to decide upon whether the marketplace massacre in Sarajevo was caused by the Muslims firing on their own sides or the Serbs. That was a subject of another trial. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I disagree. I have to use that as an example of the fact that my approach is meant to forward the interests of justice, and you implied that my approach was not forwarding the interests of justice. I certainly take profound exception to that. I am a veteran of that part of the world. I'm terribly distressed by what happened. And I feel that people to act fairly and correctly must have all the details in front of them. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So finally, your view is that if a Court is going to look at allegations of crimes committed by a Serb in Banja Luka, it should equally be looking at the same time at allegations relating to Sarajevo or elsewhere. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PAUL SHOUP [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly what I'm saying. But it's not all that I'm saying. The strategy of victimisation is one meant to deceive people. There is a great deal of deceptive information. Some of this applies to what Karadzic was doing and others in the region of Banja Luka itself. There is a tremendous propaganda operation here. I'm not taking the Serb position as, you know, "we're all misunderstood." I really reject that completely out of hand. But anything that happened that concerns the Serbs in Banja Luka or this whole region of Bosanska Krajina has to be looked at in terms of the efforts of those who want to make it look different than it really is. This is the Balkan way of doing things. You are trying to always make yourself look like the victim and to distort the actions of the other person. And I plea with the Court not to be fooled by this kind of thing. It applies to everybody, I'm sure. I say in my report that Serbs have also issued false statements. I didn't hesitate to tell you where in that tape that we saw yesterday there were mistakes, and I'll give you another example of one that I thought was an egregious error in that tape when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down. Interpreters can't follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But there's a moment -- I wonder if anybody else noticed it. There's a moment in the tape where they talk about Mostar. Perhaps I could ask you -- it's out of order to ask you. Do you remember when they talked about Mostar, and they said that the liquidation of the Serbs took place in Mostar, and then they went on to say -- and then someone came on the tape who was an expert or something and said, "This fierce fighting took place in Mostar, people were destroying each other. It was far worse than Bosnia." When you listened to tape it sounded as though it was the Serbs who had been liquidated in Mostar. Of course they weren't liquidated. They were driven out but they weren't liquidated. And the fight that this expert is talking about is between the Muslims and the Croats. That's the kind of thing you're constantly contending with on both sides in this whole procedure, and that's why I plea for careful examination of all the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We stop here for today. We are meeting tomorrow in the morning. I can't confirm the courtroom because I don't remember whether it's this courtroom or Courtroom Number II. If we are sitting in Courtroom II -- I can tell you actually; I have it here. Courtroom III, we are sitting here. So tomorrow morning at 9.00. Do you think you'll finish, Ms. Korner, tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to make it absolutely clear I will try, but the professor simply must not go on like this. Because the longer the answers, the longer he's likely to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but at least we have got the message of -- the underlying motive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour. I may well tomorrow morning ask to repeat my original submission about this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, feel free to do that, provided it's not a mere repetition of a question seeking a mere repetition of an --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, may I just mention that it has become absolutely, as you say, clear what the Professor's agenda is, and tu quoque is not a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. But I suppose Mr. Ackerman knows as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is absolutely not clear that is what his agenda is. It is not his agenda. His agenda is to give you a historical factual background from which you can make reasonable judgements. He has said it. He didn't say -- he denied that tu quoque has anything to do with what he is doing here, and he isn't. And I object to Ms. Korner making these submissions to you about her attitude about his testimony. I didn't do that with her witnesses. She shouldn't do it to mine. She should ask her questions, get her answers, and be satisfied with that. This is just getting beyond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not discuss further in the presence of the witness, Mr. Ackerman. Tomorrow morning, 9.00. I thank you and have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 6th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.53 p.m.,
